# Product and API reference

[Back to README](../README.md) · [中文说明](./product-and-api_zh.md)

This document preserves the detailed product behavior and HTTP/MCP contracts. The root README is the short project entry point; runtime architecture lives in [architecture.md](../architecture.md), while [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) only routes coding agents to the owning references.

## Notebook titles and descriptions

Notebook `name` and `purpose` have independent automatic/manual ownership. A
new notebook with a placeholder name and empty description starts with both
fields automatic. Supplying a custom name or nonempty description at creation
makes that field manual. An explicit PATCH of either field makes only that field
manual, including clearing a description or setting a placeholder name; automatic
refresh never overwrites it. The settings form omits untouched fields, and the
workspace title follows automatic updates without replacing an in-progress edit.

Offline `batch ingest`, `batch all`, and `batch reparse` skip automatic notebook
name/description refresh by default, including failed sources, with no final
refresh. Existing field values and automatic/manual ownership remain unchanged;
later online source operations can refresh automatic fields as usual. Source
summaries, paper metadata, and embedding retain their behavior, as does KG
extraction in `batch all` and `batch reparse`.
These phases (and `batch kg`) also skip the per-source automatic scale-index
build/fold queueing and the agent-understanding consolidation trigger (the trigger
counter still accumulates, so consolidation runs at the notebook's next source
change or a manual rebuild). `batch ingest` never extracts KG, even into a notebook
that already has one: run `batch kg` afterwards. `batch kg` and `batch all` rebuild
the unified KG at their end and rebuild the scale index only for a base-tier
notebook or one that already has an index.

Source type corrections refresh automatic fields as well. Online source parsing/reparsing refreshes automatic fields after the source summary is
stored; a failed parse also refreshes, using that source's title without its error
text. Failure handling clears any previously stored summary without changing
the current processing state, refreshes metadata, then publishes terminal failure
so polling readers observe the final metadata. Deletion refreshes after the source row is removed, before returning. The
input includes every visible local source's title, document type and available
summary, in stable creation order; hidden Memory/Knowhow projections and mounted
reference libraries are excluded. Pending sources contribute titles until their
summaries become available. This is synthesis of source metadata, not full-text
reading: source-summary generation retains its existing document projection.

All source metadata participates, including summaries beyond the old prefix and
sources beyond the old first-source window. Large inputs use bounded batches and
recursive summary merging; no source-count cutoff applies. Stable source groups
opt into the existing LLM response cache with the same strict output validator
used at publication. An append or a newly ready summary reuses unchanged groups
and recomputes affected ancestors; cache entries retain the shared cache's
endpoint/model/parameter/prompt keys, size and expiry policy. Disabling or evicting
that cache increases model work but does not change corpus coverage. Concurrent requests
within one runtime coalesce, and participating ingestion/deletion calls wait for
the final refresh before their completion response. A database generation plus
field ownership guards rejects superseded responses and concurrent manual edits.
Unavailable/failed model calls use a deterministic count/type description; a
multi-source fallback title describes the collection instead of its first source.
Deleting the last source resets only automatic fields to the empty-library text.

Metadata generation rails (do not apply to user-authored fields):

| Rail | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `NOTEBOOK_METADATA_BATCH_CHARS` | default 12000, range 4096–100000; source/partial-summary characters per model input batch, excluding the fixed prompt |
| `NOTEBOOK_METADATA_BATCH_SOURCES` | default 16, range 2–128; stable group size for recursive merging, not a corpus source-count limit |
| `NOTEBOOK_AUTO_NAME_MAX_CHARS` | 120; longer model output rejects the pass instead of silently truncating |
| `NOTEBOOK_AUTO_DESCRIPTION_MAX_CHARS` | 1000; longer model output rejects the pass instead of silently truncating |

SQLite v75 / PostgreSQL 0055 conservatively preserves all legacy non-placeholder
titles because older databases did not record title ownership; only legacy
placeholder titles become automatic. Existing description ownership is retained.
There is no inferred reclassification or startup model backfill. Copies preserve
field ownership, except an explicitly supplied copy name becomes manual.

## Current Scope

Silicon Notebook is a team knowledge workspace with a FastAPI backend and a Next.js frontend.
PostgreSQL 16 is the default deployment backend; SQLite remains supported. Each deployment
selects one database through `DATABASE_URL` (no dual-write/dual-read mode). Installation,
model services, offline fallbacks and the non-Docker deployment workflow are documented in
[Deployment and configuration](./deployment-and-configuration.md).

- [Source uploads and parsing](#source-uploads-and-parsing): documents, workbooks and Markdown image bundles; background ingestion and visible quality warnings.
- [Product Flow](#product-flow): notebooks, grounded Ask, knowledge browsing, private Memory and Deep Reports.
- [Accounts and usage](#accounts-and-usage), [group sharing](#group-knowledge-sharing), and [external authentication](#external-authentication).
- [Retrieval modes](#retrieval-modes-ask): general Q&A and iterative reasoning, with [user-selected source scope](#source-selected-retrieval-scope).
- [Knowhow tables](#knowhow-tables) and [Memory / Agent MCP](#memory-and-agent-mcp).
- [Deep Report lifecycle](#deep-report-lifecycle-and-execution-limits), [public report sharing](#public-report-share-guardrails), and [public conversation sharing](#public-conversation-share-guardrails).
- [Global Ask](#global-ask), [API routes](#apis), and [current limitations](#current-limitations).

A fresh database seeds the local administrator, with no demo notebooks or synthetic sources.

## Source uploads and parsing

- Multipart source upload for PDF, Markdown, Markdown ZIP bundles, DOCX, PPTX, CSV, XLSX, and legacy binary XLS (async through the shared KG job scheduler). The add-source dialog middle-compacts overlong staged filenames while retaining the ending/extension and full-name tooltip. Drag-drop and the file picker share one staging path; files skipped at staging time (unsupported type — with a save-as hint for legacy Office formats, over the per-file size cap, or over the batch cap) are listed persistently inside the dialog with per-file reasons instead of being silently filtered by the browser's `accept` attribute or flashed in a transient toast. It includes the whole staged batch in the effective document-limit check: a batch larger than the remaining allowance is disabled before submission and accompanied by the remaining/excess counts and an actionable remedy. Staging a standalone `.md`/`.markdown` also scans its image targets: local/relative targets produce a persistent advisory to upload a ZIP or drop the complete folder, and remote targets disclose that the server does not fetch them. The warning never blocks the still-useful text upload and does not apply to ZIP/folder bundle intake. Advisory reads are sequential across the batch, and an asynchronously completed row is admitted only while that exact name+size file remains staged.

- **KG-native ingestion**: structured Markdown parse → greedy-window KG extraction (Concept / Claim / Formula / Procedure) with concurrent embedding → extraction-first status (`extracted` = KG ready, does not wait for embedding)

MinerU parses PDF/DOCX/PPTX/XLSX when configured. An unavailable or unusable result follows these local fallback chains:

| Format | Local parsing and limitation |
| --- | --- |
| PDF | PyMuPDF4LLM layout-aware Markdown, then pypdf. |
| DOCX | mammoth preserves headings, lists and tables (`table_html` metadata) and equations (as LaTeX, see below), then flat python-docx extraction. Inline images are not persisted; base64 image URIs are discarded. |
| PPTX | python-pptx preserves slide tables, chart titles, grouped shapes, speaker notes and equations (as LaTeX, see below), then raw slide XML. Pictures are not persisted. |
| XLSX/XLSM | openpyxl retains all cell values. |
| Legacy binary XLS | Always `xlrd`; no MinerU path. |
| Legacy DOC/PPT | Unsupported; save as DOCX/PPTX first. |

Lossy PDF/DOCX/PPTX fallback sets `parse_quality_warning` while retaining `extracted` status; workbooks do not receive this warning. A nonempty MinerU workbook result, including cloud uploads, must cover at least **0.8** of both nonempty rows and cells (`MINERU_WORKBOOK_MIN_ROW_COVERAGE` in `parsers.py`). Non-table text contributes at most one row and cell; images contribute neither. Failure on either dimension discards the result for openpyxl. Image assets are persisted only after acceptance.

Overlong tables from XLSX/DOCX/PPTX sources (PDF tables are naturally bounded by their rendered page and are unaffected) are split on row boundaries during parsing, capped by both row count (≤30) and character count — the character cap is `CHUNK_TARGET_CHARS` itself (the same target the plain-text chunker uses; no separate setting), whichever limit is hit first, with an overlong single row still kept as one part. A detected title/header block never gets split across parts: it stays whole in part 1 even if that pushes part 1 over the character cap. Retrieval text for part 2+ is prefixed with the detected header row's flattened text, unless the header text itself is longer than half the character cap (a very wide header would otherwise eat most of the segment's budget). A part whose own body text is empty (e.g. a trailing run of blank rows) is dropped rather than emitted as a caption/header-only element, and the surviving parts are renumbered so `table_part` stays contiguous starting at 1. `CHUNK_TARGET_CHARS` should stay comfortably below `EMBED_TRUNCATE_CHARS`; otherwise a header-bearing segment can still be truncated before it reaches the embedding model.

Each split-off table element carries `metadata.table_group` (identical across all parts of the same table, equal to the unsuffixed label), `metadata.table_part` (1-based, contiguous), and `metadata.table_parts` (the total after empty-part filtering). Only part 1's `table_html` contains the header row; later parts hold only their own rows. The source detail view merges a run of consecutive elements sharing `table_group` with strictly increasing `table_part` back into a single rendered table with one header row. Already-ingested files need to be re-parsed to pick up the new granularity.

The DOCX/PPTX local fallbacks convert Office equations (OMML: inline `m:oMath`, display `m:oMathPara`) to LaTeX deterministically (`backend/app/services/omml.py`, no new dependency), following MinerU's formula convention so retrieval, KG Formula extraction and the frontend's KaTeX rendering need no change: each line of a display equation becomes one `formula` element whose text is bare LaTeX (no delimiters), with `metadata.text_format` set to `latex` and the label `DOCX formula N` / `PPTX slide S formula N`, and the surrounding paragraph or text box is split around it; inline equations stay in the paragraph/slide text as `$…$`. Headings, list items, table cells (escaped inside `table_html`) and speaker notes are never split, so a display equation inside one of them is kept inline as `$…$` too; the last-resort extractors (python-docx, raw slide XML) keep every equation inline and never emit separate elements. PowerPoint stores each equation text box inside `mc:AlternateContent`, which python-pptx never yielded, so such a box used to vanish together with any other text in it; only alternates whose Choice holds math are opened now, every other AlternateContent behaves as before. The converter covers fractions, sub/superscripts, radicals, n-ary operators (∑ ∫ ∏ …), delimiters, matrices, functions, accents, over/underbars, group characters, lower/upper limits, equation arrays and the common symbols; an unknown construct degrades to its text, and conversion never raises or drops text. Math-free documents parse byte-for-byte as before. Already-ingested DOCX/PPTX sources need to be re-parsed to gain their equations; sources MinerU parsed successfully are unaffected (MinerU supplies the formulas).

Known trade-off: the collection map's table count and the agentic enumeration tools count/list a split table once (its part 1), not once per part — a continuation part is identified by its `location_label` ending in " part N" (N ≥ 2), the same convention `_split_table_into_elements` uses to name the parts. Enumeration likewise returns only part 1; a later part is not separately browsable, but its content is still reachable through ordinary chunk retrieval and citation.

MinerU images appear inline and their captions remain searchable. Markdown image `alt` becomes `metadata.caption` and enters chunk retrieval. A plain-path image with neither alt nor a qualifying description produces no element.

Whole-paragraph `data:image/{png,jpeg,gif,webp};base64,...` images can be persisted through the source-image asset port. Unrecognized MIME types (including svg/bmp/avif) are not admitted. The literal data URI is stripped to alt text in every position—including mixed paragraphs, lists, headings and table cells—and never enters element metadata. Only whole-paragraph images are persisted; other positions retain alt text only. Persistence uses `MINERU_MAX_IMAGE_BYTES` (default 5 MB), `MINERU_MAX_IMAGES_PER_SOURCE` (default 200), and `MINERU_RETURN_IMAGES` (false disables all source-image persistence). An alt-less data image that cannot persist and has no description produces no element.

An immediately following blockquote can supply `metadata.description`, joined to the caption for searchable element text and used as the citation-image caption fallback. A blank separator is allowed; a link-reference definition or other intervening source content is not. Its first line must be only the **图片描述** marker (bold and a trailing colon optional), or that marker followed by a colon and text; “图片描述如下” does not qualify. The block must contain visibly nonblank description text and no fenced/indented code or HTML block. Lists, headings, tables and nested quotes are included. Marker-only, `<br>`-only or empty-alt-only quotes remain ordinary quotes.

The description creates one image element, without a duplicate paragraph element; KG extraction still reads its original source slice. Multi-paragraph descriptions are not split by the 600-character chunker: embedding retains its configured input-length limit while lexical retrieval sees the full text. The citation caption retains its ordinary cap. Local image files can be converted to data URIs with [`embed_md_images.py`](../scripts/embed_md_images.py).

- **Markdown + image bundle upload**: `.zip` is a first-class built-in parser format. The browser uploads the raw archive unchanged; it is stored as one source and parsed in the background, independent of MinerU. Every `.md`/`.markdown` member is parsed in stable archive-path order and tagged with `metadata.bundle_path`. A local image target is URL-decoded, stripped of query/fragment suffixes, resolved relative to the Markdown member that references it (archive-root paths also work), then admitted by png/jpeg/gif/webp magic bytes and persisted through the ordinary source-image asset port. The archive is never extracted to the host filesystem. Unsafe or duplicate paths, encryption, unsupported compression, no Markdown member, too many retained files, corruption, and an aggregate uncompressed size over the ordinary per-source upload ceiling reject the source as a whole. A missing, remote, corrupt, or unsupported image is a per-image fail-open: its original `src` and caption/description text remain, so the image element is searchable when it has caption/description but renders without an `<img>`. The existing image-storage switch and per-image/per-source asset rails still apply at persistence time. A dropped **folder** remains the compatibility path through the dependency-free browser pipeline (`frontend/app/md-bundle.ts` / `bundle-intake.ts`): it resolves relative paths, magic-sniffs and data-URI-inlines supported images, and keeps its persistent five-category pairing receipt and deliberately conservative whole-paragraph/image-description checks. Exact backend-ZIP and browser-folder guardrails are registered in the [table below](#markdown-bundle-upload-guardrails).

### Navigation-page detection

When a source is chunked, chunks that are navigation pages — a table of contents, a list of figures or
tables — are marked (`chunks.navigation`) and kept out of retrieval ranking. The judgement uses only the
source's own headings, never label words or line patterns. Titles and chunk text are normalised alike
(NFKC, case-folded, only letters, digits and CJK characters kept); a heading takes part only when its title,
without a leading enumerator such as `5.7.2.1`, `Figure 1-1.` or `A.2` (else the full title), is at least
**10** weighted characters long, a CJK character weighing **3** (so `Overview` / `概述` do not take part,
`5.7.2.1损耗` does). In a chunk, the *hits* are the titles of other headings it contains (not its own
section or that section's ancestors; a title wholly inside a longer one counts once) and the *chain* is the
longest run of hits in document order. A chunk is a navigation page when all five hold:

| Condition | Threshold | What it separates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| References: titles on the chain | ≥ **6** | a few cross-references in body text |
| Order ratio: chain / distinct hits | ≥ **0.75** | a table of section titles in another order |
| Letter coverage: share of the non-digit characters inside hits | ≥ **0.65** | prose that names the sections one sentence each |
| Locality: share of the chain inside the chunk's own section subtree or its parent's (a parent that is the document's common root does not count; `Figure 5-1`, `Chapter 5` and `第5章` belong to chapter 5, `Figure A-1` and `Appendix A` to appendix A; numbering and breadcrumbs both count; 0 when the document has neither) | < **0.5** | a chapter's opening overview, a summary or register table of its own subsections |
| Density: chain / same-kind headings between the chain's first and last heading (numbered titles down to the chain's deepest level, captions by their leading word, breadcrumb titles by depth) | ≥ **0.6** | a revision history or summary citing one section per chapter |

A summary that lists *whole* subtrees of other chapters (an appendix register summary, say) meets all five
and is marked. A source with more than **5000** headings is not judged (its chunks stay unmarked).
`NAVIGATION_DETECTION_ENABLED` (default `true`) switches the judgement off; operations:
[Navigation-page marker backfill](./operations.md#navigation-page-marker-backfill-scriptsbackfill_navigation_chunkspy).

Table-of-contents and list-of-figures/tables pages are not retrieval evidence. A marked chunk is removed —
not ranked lower — at every place retrieval turns stored chunks into candidates: chunk scoring (vector,
lexical, keyword and generated-question arms), PPR, KG source passages, the exact-identifier channel (a
marked hit opens no section, and a marked chunk in a fetched section is skipped), the selected-source graph
lane, chunks an extension proposes, and a report follow-up's restored citations (a flagged passage and the elements it lists do not read back and count as gone). It takes no slot of the final selection (the candidate limit, MMR,
the PPR ceiling walk's slots, the exact channel's section slots); upstream recall windows it may have
occupied before being removed are not widened to make up for it — the ANN/FTS recall windows, the first
`ppr_top_chunks` PPR passages without a source ceiling (and the selected-source graph's online PPR
`max_results`), the exact probe window and each fetched section's chunk cap — so those legs can return
fewer passages. The element arm likewise drops every element a marked chunk lists, read from the marked
chunks themselves (an element a marked chunk shares with a body chunk is dropped too). The marked chunk
still counts toward the source-ceiling check of the candidate pool. `RETRIEVAL_NAVIGATION_FILTER_ENABLED` (default `true`) is the read-side switch: `false`
keeps marked chunks and elements everywhere, restoring the results from before the marker, without
touching the stored flags.

## Accounts and usage

The login screen centers a single notebook cover, sharing the application's background, panel, text, accent, border and shadow tokens and system font. The cover keeps only the Silicon Notebook name, SN mark, book icon and deployment-selected sign-in controls; surrounding slogans and footer copy are absent. Under unified authentication the resting screen has one sign-in button. Required local-credential controls and actionable failure messages remain available; the successful-entry announcement is screen-reader-only.

The login screen presents a notebook cover with the deployment-selected sign-in controls. Successful local login/registration and SSO completion (including account linking/creation) open the cover and turn its pages to reveal the application. This transition plays once for that sign-in, does not replay on an ordinary session refresh, and is bypassed when the system requests reduced motion. The application loads underneath the transition; its controls remain inert until the short animation ends, with a timeout fallback so animation events cannot block entry.

Local authentication supports registration with one letter followed by eight digits (for example `a12345678`, stored lowercase), password login and opaque Bearer sessions. These controls are available only while [external authentication](#external-authentication) is off. Users see owned notebooks and large shared notebooks they explicitly joined. The built-in `admin` is seeded on first boot and owns legacy notebooks; its password comes from `SILICON_NOTEBOOK_ADMIN_PASSWORD` (local default `admin`, which must change for production/non-loopback startup). `SILICON_NOTEBOOK_AUTH_OPTIONAL=true` is for local/no-auth testing.

| Account operation | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `PATCH /api/admin/users/{user_id}/role` | Grant/revoke administrator role; the built-in administrator and the caller's own admin role are protected. Existing sessions observe changes on their next request. |
| `PATCH /api/me/password` with `{old_password, new_password}` | Wrong current password or blank replacement: 400. Success retains the requesting session and revokes the user's other browser sessions. |
| `POST /api/admin/users/{user_id}/reset-password` with `{new_password}` | Requires a real administrator session (anonymous `auth_optional` fallback: 403); revokes all target browser sessions. |
| Password change/reset for built-in `admin` | 409; change the environment setting and restart. The UI hides self-change and marks this account protected. |

Password changes/resets leave Agent long-lived credentials unchanged. The browser exposes login/registration as policy permits, plus the current username and logout.

When a session is rejected (`/me` returns 401: expired, revoked, or a local session after unified authentication was switched on), the browser clears only the credential that was rejected, keeping a session another tab switched in meanwhile, and returns to the login page. The workspace (`/`) handles this in its own startup; standalone pages (user usage overview, question analysis, loaded extensions, Agent access, update history, wish wall, log viewer and global Q&A) share one entry that opens the login page as `/?next=<this page>`, staying in their loading state until the navigation completes instead of showing "登录状态已失效". After local login, registration or unified authentication (including account linking/creation) the user returns to that page with its path, query and hash; a valid session restored on a login page carrying `next` goes straight there too. `next` accepts only a validated same-site relative path: external, protocol-relative, backslash- or control-character-bearing locations and the unified-authentication callback page are ignored and removed from the address bar. Other failures (server errors, network loss) keep the credential, and the page keeps its existing error and retry.

The user-usage page renders registration dates, last activity, last seen, notebook timestamps, and Parsing issues update and cleanup times in the browser's current timezone, matching Question analysis. Offset-bearing timestamps are converted before extracting the date, including across midnight and daylight-saving transitions; legacy timestamps without an offset retain their local-time interpretation. Missing or invalid values display `—`.

The user-usage page sorts the complete `GET /api/admin/users` result before pagination (default 20 rows; choices 20/50/100; sortable data-column headers). Expanding a user shows a summary and the complete owner-only `GET /api/admin/users/{user_id}/notebooks` inventory, paginated at 20 notebooks per page. Overview totals include that user's activity in shared notebooks and retained activity from deleted notebooks; the owned-notebook breakdown can therefore differ from the total:

| Field | Attribution and scope |
| --- | --- |
| `questions` | User-owned `ask_jobs` submissions in every status, including failed/cancelled, plus `global_ask_jobs`; not conversation containers or other members' questions. Global jobs have no per-notebook breakdown. |
| Report total | Report creator, including reports in shared notebooks. |
| `sources` / `storage_bytes` | Visible source count / sum of `file_size`; live notebooks use `COALESCE(uploaded_by, notebook.created_by)`. Retained sources from deleted notebooks use the retained actor, falling back to the owner at deletion. The notebook breakdown counts all visible sources in each owned notebook, regardless of uploader. |
| `last_active` | Latest `created_at` of a visible upload, Ask submission (including global) or report creation, including retained deleted-notebook activity. Background updates and synthetic Memory/Knowhow sources do not refresh it. |
| `last_seen` | `users.last_seen_at`: login and subsequent authenticated browser requests, throttled by `AUTH_SESSION_TOUCH_INTERVAL_SECONDS`; survives logout/revocation. Agent credentials do not refresh it; null means unseen since the column was introduced. |
| `questions_30d` | Notebook/global Ask submissions, including retained records, in the trailing 30 days. |
| `questions_failed` / `reports_failed` | Only `status='failed'`, including retained activity and global Ask; cancelled is excluded. |
| `kg_builds` | User-created KG jobs in every status; not retained after notebook deletion. |
| `memory_count` | User's Memory in live notebooks, excluding `rejected`. |
| `knowhow_tables` | Tables created by the user in live notebooks, including deep-copy replicas attributed to the copier. |
| `joined_notebooks` / `groups` | Membership in other users' live shared notebooks / groups. |
| `conversations` | Deprecated compatibility field; includes the user's global conversations. |

An actual upload refreshes its submitting user's `last_active`, including into another owner's shared notebook. A deep copy refreshes neither uploader nor recipient; a copy's null `uploaded_by` still falls back to the notebook owner for asset totals. Pre-tracking upload activity is best-effort attributed to the historical notebook owner.

Expanded summaries add no main-table column or sort key: one line shows last seen, storage, 30-day questions, question/report totals with nonzero failure counts, and KG builds (「图谱整理」); the second shows Memory, Knowhow, joined notebooks and groups. Missing last seen renders 「—」. Storage uses base-1024 KB/MB/GB/TB with one decimal, or integer bytes below 1 KB.

Each notebook limits uploaded documents to `USER_UPLOAD_DOCUMENT_LIMIT` (default 20); administrator-owned notebooks are exempt. Administrators manage the global default through `PATCH /api/admin/settings/upload-limit-default` and per-user overrides through `PATCH /api/admin/users/{user_id}/upload-limit` (`null` restores inheritance). Administrators can publish public base libraries: these are hidden from ordinary users' notebook lists but available in the reference picker, and participate only after an explicit mount. Legacy schema-20 upgrades create no mounts automatically.

- **Share links**: owners can publish an opaque notebook link. Small notebooks are copied into the recipient's account; large notebooks are joined as read-only membership. Write access stays with the owner, and there is no live collaborative editing.

## Global Ask

Global Ask opens from a bottom-right bubble in the authenticated collection and notebook workspace.
On the collection page the bubble is a labelled pill (icon plus 「全局问答」, 124×48px) so people can tell
what it is without hovering; inside a notebook workspace the label folds away and the pill animates down to
a 40px circle tucked into the empty corner below-right of the Ask composer — the composer never makes room
for it, so its left and right margins stay symmetric. The first time a user sees the collection page, a
one-time hint above the pill says what Global Ask does; it never takes focus, and it is retired for that user
(remembered in the browser's local storage) once they dismiss it, open Global Ask, or leave the list after
seeing it.
Clicking opens a compact chat; expanding fills the viewport with history and chat.
Minimizing, reopening and switching size retain the same mounted conversation, draft, scope and task
progress; minimizing does not cancel a task. Embedded chat leaves the host URL unchanged and loads
its data only after first opening. Reopening refreshes notebook choices without resetting the chat;
error recovery restores the active conversation, draft scope and running-task polling. Signing out clears its local state. `/ask` remains independently
accessible, including conversation links. Conversations belong to the initiating user; they neither create an empty carrier notebook
nor change reference-library mounts. The page reuses the shared header, palette, button feedback and
answer Markdown, with conversation history, searchable notebook selection, a persistent scope summary,
background-task status. Citations use the same card as in-notebook Ask: clicking an inline marker opens
it beside the marker with the cited passage, its notebook and library tier, plus an **open notebook** link
that goes to that notebook at the cited source (a plain click also minimizes the chat; a modified click
opens a new tab and leaves it open). There is no citation list under the answer and no side reader; entries
that need a notebook workspace (source view, Knowledge Graph, Knowhow row, import) are absent.
Attached images do appear — both the inline citation-image blocks in the body and the **attached images**
strip inside the citation card — and clicking one opens the same page-level zoom preview as notebook Ask (the
same `answer-image-preview` root-modal seat, zoom and stepping; the gallery may span notebooks) in the compact
window, the full window and the standalone `/ask` page alike. Each image is read through the
asset endpoint of the notebook that owns its citation — the preview reads each image through that same
notebook — and every request re-checks the current user's read
access to that notebook and that the asset's owning library is in that notebook's effective participant set.
In-notebook Ask still proxies through the active notebook, unchanged. In the floating window the modal
coordinator opens the preview as a **child layer** stacked over the window (policy `stacksOver`): the window
stays, only leaving the interaction tree (the full window temporarily drops to non-modal), Escape, the backdrop
and the close button close only the preview and focus returns to the image that opened it, and only the next
Escape collapses the window as before; if the window leaves, the preview leaves with it. The coordinator
counts key presses: one Escape press closes at most one layer (holding Escape down still closes only one), even if the browser still sends a close request to
the window it just revealed; the press a citation card or the share dialog consumes counts the same way. While the preview covers the full window, focus stays in whatever layer is topmost at that moment (a dialog such as
the release notes that pops up over the preview, then the preview again once it closes) and Tab cannot
reach the hidden page; over the compact window there is no focus trap, as in notebook Ask.
While a card is open, Escape closes only the card (an image opened from the card closes first, then the card). The mobile layout retains scope, send and stop.
The question appears in the transcript at the moment it is sent (the same instant as the notebook Ask's
pending turn); for `reasoning`, the understanding steps run live under it, using the same client-synthesized
steps as the notebook Ask, and are prepended to the job's own live trace once the job exists; a cancelled or
failed attempt returns the question to the input.
The browser follows a running job through the push stream (`GET /jobs/{job_id}/stream`), and falls back to
polling when that stream never opens, errors, or ends without a terminal frame. A hidden document keeps the
stream running — it is push, so there is nothing to pause. That fallback polling backs off from 1.2 seconds
to 15 seconds while progress is unchanged, pauses when the browser
document is hidden, and resumes immediately on visibility; a change in the coverage receipts **or in the
number of trace steps** counts as progress, so a reasoning run that keeps emitting steps stays at 1.2 seconds. Narrowing scope shows a history-context reminder.
Ungrounded answers carry an explicit warning even when they include some citations. Each completed or
skipped notebook persists a narrow coverage update, so polling and mid-retrieval cancellation retain progress.

Global Ask and in-notebook Ask run on the SAME engine, and the composer offers the same engine picker:
`reasoning` (the default) and `chunk`. Deployment extension engines are absent from that picker and the
backend rejects them with 422; an unrecognized `mode` is rejected the same way. A finished job returns the
standard answer shape in-notebook Ask returns (field `answer`); jobs written before this unification keep
the legacy shape (field `response`) read-only, and answer text, citations and reasoning trace are read
through one projection that covers both. The answer is never written into any notebook's answer records; it
lives only in the global conversation and job. A `reasoning` submission first runs a corpus-blind
understanding preflight whose result is shown for review, and only the confirmed understanding is submitted;
the reasoning trace appears step by step while the job runs, and the answer's own trace is authoritative once
it finishes. `retrieval_effort` is always `standard` in global Ask v1: a request carrying `deep` runs at
`standard` and the interface offers no level — the deep round count multiplied by eight libraries does not
fit the retrieval phase budget and would report most libraries as never searched.

**Record parity**: a global Ask job leaves the **same record** a notebook Ask job leaves; the only
difference is how it retrieves. Each job records: the question, the engine (`mode`), status, the answer
(with citations and reasoning trace), the submission instant `asked_at`, the last-transition instant
`updated_at`, this turn's submission surface `submitted_via`, and the rating `feedback` plus the instant it
was written `feedback_at` (first write wins). The rating lives only on the global job and is not
written to the notebook `feedback` table; the statistics read across both: the notebook analytics panel
and the admin Question Analysis count 👍/👎 from the `feedback` table and from rated global jobs (see
Question Analysis below and `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/analytics`), finding the rated jobs through a partial
index that holds only rated rows (SQLite v96 / PostgreSQL 0076 `idx_global_ask_jobs_feedback`), so an
unrated job is never read. When a job turns `done`, the same transaction records its **attribution**: one
`global_ask_job_notebooks(job_id, notebook_id)` row per attributed notebook (searched ∪ cited; when both are
empty, the participants minus the skipped ones — the post-Ask learning chain's rule,
`global_ask_attribution`) and `global_ask_jobs.attributed = 1` (SQLite v98 / PostgreSQL 0078); a failed,
cancelled or interrupted job writes none. Deleting a job (retention purge, conversation delete) deletes its
attribution rows. Jobs finished before the upgrade carry `attributed = 0` and no rows; a background pass
started once the service is ready writes them (`scripts/backfill_global_ask_attribution.py` re-runs it by
hand; see Operations, "Global Ask attribution backfill"), and until it has caught up the statistics keep
reading those jobs through the old payload predicate, so the counts do not change. A failure additionally records the raw exception text,
readable by administrators only — the owner still sees the fixed Chinese sentence. The request body gains
an optional `asked_at` field, following the same rule as the notebook `AskRequest.asked_at`: empty, or an
ISO-8601 instant with a timezone offset; it is not part of the idempotent request's identity.
`submitted_via` is written only by the server entry point: the web route `POST /api/global-ask/ask`
always records `web`, the MCP tool `ask` always records `mcp`. On rows created before these fields
existed, `asked_at`/`updated_at`/the raw failure text stay empty and are not reconstructed;
`submitted_via` is backfilled from the value its conversation had already recorded.

**Post-completion learning chains**: once a global Ask job is persisted `done`, it advances the **same three** background chains a notebook Ask advances, attributed the way a cross-library run can be: the notebook-understanding overlay chain counts one "this member finished an Ask in this notebook" **per library the run actually retrieved from or cited** (a run that made no federated call at all counts its participants minus the skipped ones), and its trace sample reads, under that same attribution rule, the member's global asks attributed to that library alongside their notebook asks (a library the run resolved but neither retrieved from nor cited never sees the run); the retrieval-experience library counts one ask into the **global partition** only (`reasoning` runs only) — a federated run's tactics describe no single library, and a global run injects from the global partition only (the anchor library is a name, not a partition it reads); the search-profile inference counts one ask per person. Cancelled and failed jobs count for nothing; a completed job that retrieved from no library at all (every leg skipped) still counts for the person's search profile and the global experience partition and still reaches the observers, only the overlay has no library to count. A deployment extension on `ask.completed_observer` receives **one** notification (as for a notebook Ask): every observer's context carries `scope="global"`; an observer holding the agent-profile notification capability additionally gets `notebook` (the anchor: the run's `nominal_active`, not necessarily among the counted libraries) and `notebooks` (the libraries counted this time, possibly empty), while every other capability sees an empty `notebooks` — the same identity-projection rule under which they already see no `notebook`.

Scope has two states: `all` means every currently readable notebook; `include` is an explicit set.
Clearing selection restores `all`. Manually selecting every current notebook remains an explicit set,
whereas `all` resolves current access again on the next turn. Omitting scope starts a new conversation
with `all`, or inherits the current scope on follow-up; the browser explicitly sends its selection each
turn. An invalid or inaccessible explicit notebook rejects the request instead of silently disappearing.
Mounts never expand the participant set. Execution freezes participants and source ceilings, so notebooks
or sources added later cannot join a running request.
**A scope with nothing to search is refused at submission**, by the single-library "retrieval scope is
empty" composition applied per participant over what a global run can actually search: its retrieval
universe is the participants' frozen visible-source lists, and hidden Knowhow/Memory projections or
knowledge objects whose evidence lies outside them are never retrievable by a global run. So **any**
participant with a non-empty frozen list admits the request, and only an all-empty set is refused; a
library holding only Knowhow cells, confirmed Memory or knowledge objects does not count. Mounted
libraries do not count either (the participant set never grows along mounts). The check reads only the
participants this viewer may read in this request (for MCP, also intersected with the token allowlist),
after the read re-check; naming an unreadable library is still a 404 whether or not it holds content. The
refusal lands before any conversation or job exists and the `reasoning` intent preview refuses too, so no
model call is spent: HTTP 409 whose `detail` is the user-message-marked Chinese sentence
「当前检索范围为空：范围内的笔记本还没有可检索的内容，请换选有资料的笔记本，或先添加来源。」 (the single-library
409's shape and opening); the streaming preview carries it as the `error` frame's `status` + `message`;
MCP `ask` returns `unavailable` with the same sentence (the code the single-notebook path gives an empty
notebook). In the UI the sentence appears in the notice strip directly above the input, without the
「重新加载」 button, and the question returns to the input. The check reads only the already-frozen lists
and adds no query.

Browser scope follows the user's live read access; MCP additionally intersects the live token allowlist.
History, task results and cited evidence recheck access. Narrowing scope cannot reintroduce excluded
notebook material through earlier assistant answers. Receipts distinguish eligible participants, notebooks
actually searched, skipped notebooks with Chinese reasons, notebooks whose retrieval partly failed, and
notebooks cited. A `reasoning` job federates once per retrieval round, and receipts are folded over the WHOLE
job: a notebook is reported skipped only when NO round succeeded (carrying the most recent round's reason),
one that answered somewhere and failed somewhere is reported degraded, and empty retrieval still counts as
searched. Degraded therefore now means only "some of this notebook's retrieval legs failed"; it is no longer
the per-notebook signal for lexical fallback. A job that made no federated call at all — a document overview
or a collection enumeration answers straight from the enumeration lanes — reports no notebook as skipped.
A skip reason states only what happened and never guesses a cause such as a broken index: only a
retrieval that actually ran out of time asks the user to narrow scope, a notebook still queued when the phase
budget expired says retrieval never started, and everything else asks them to retry. The machine-readable cause
travels as a content-free `chunk_federation_skipped` event instead. Authorization changes still fail closed. Not citing a notebook does not assert absence of material.
Only completed, scope-compatible turns enter follow-up context through shared query rewriting; assistant answers
resolve references but are never evidence. Submission freezes each participant's currently visible source list,
and once the answer exists every citation AND every answer anchor naming library material is rechecked — each
one on its own, never stopping at the first failure. The recheck judges citation INTEGRITY only; permission and
source-scope enforcement belong to the retrieval layer, so no verdict ever withholds, blanks or trims answer text.
A reference is compared with its retrieval-time snapshot: the text fingerprint an evidence producer registered
when the run read it. The federated chunk channel registers it out of the SAME database snapshot as the passage
the run retrieved, and only when that passage's own text still matches what the run read (element ids are reused
deterministically when a source is re-ingested, so a fingerprint read by id alone could describe text that
replaced what the answer rested on); the other producers register through `evidence_attestation` — the text they
read hashed in-process, or one bounded by-id read for evidence they cite without reading it; the mix branch's
knowledge-graph overlay passages are registered exactly like federated passages. The first real snapshot in a
run wins, and a snapshot from a by-id read that saw no text never replaces an existing entry -- not even a
producer's statement that the text it read could not be vouched for; only a producer that read the text may
replace that. An element some producer registered in the run and that is then deleted during it keeps its card
and is reported 「资料已删除」. The check covers the WHOLE passage behind a citation, not only the element the card
names: a passage is assembled from several source elements and the rest are rechecked beside the first. Each
failed reference is marked with one of three reasons — `changed` (原文已改动: the snapshot and the current text
differ, or part of the passage is gone), `source_gone` (资料已删除: the source or the cited element was deleted;
in a global run a source leaves the frozen visible list only by deletion) or `unverifiable` (无法核对: nobody
registered a snapshot, the snapshot or the terminal read failed, or the reference names no library or a source
outside the frozen ceiling — the last two can only be retrieval-layer defects and raise a content-free
diagnostic event). Only a real snapshot mismatch is ever called a change. A reference with no source and no
element (a bare graph node, a memory row) and URL-backed external material have nothing to check. A partially
failed answer is DELIVERED WHOLE: the answer text, citations, anchors and attachments stay as the engine
produced them; the failed references carry `verification`, the answer carries `citation_check` (`outcome`
`partial`, `checked`, `failed` and the three per-kind counts, present only when `failed > 0`), `grounded`
becomes false and `evidence_level` is capped at `overview` (`inferred` is not raised). The reader sees one
sentence under the answer — 「本次回答有部分引用未通过核对：{N 条原文已改动、N 条资料已删除、N 条无法核对}。
回答内容照常保留，带标记的引用可点开查看原因。」 — and a reason line on each marked card; a reasoning run's trace
ends with a `citation_check` step stating how many citations were checked and how many failed, when the answer
has references that can be checked (an answer citing only external material or memory rows gets no such step). Both fields are
additive and omitted when empty, so single-notebook responses serialize exactly as before. They persist in the
job's payload with no migration; a row the previous recheck voided keeps its stored retry sentence. A partially
failed answer still feeds the post-completion learning chains.
An element that no longer exists when it is retrieved produces no citation card, in single-notebook and global
answers alike: a card whose subject is that element is not shown (in a single-notebook answer its `[k]` marker
is also removed from the text), a knowledge-object or derivation-chain anchor keeps its card and falls back to
the source level (it opens the source, not the element), and a table-analysis receipt falls back to the source
level as well. A single-notebook answer pays one bounded existence read for this when it cites any element and
none otherwise; a global answer learns it at retrieval time. A table-analysis receipt with no result rows
still names the library it came from, so it is checked at the source level.

Cross-notebook retrieval runs through the federated original-text channel: the participants × sub-queries task
table is submitted to a process-level shared executor rather than polled notebook by notebook. A notebook
without a knowledge graph still participates; ordinary participant notebooks are peer evidence and conflicts
retain provenance and applicability. Retrieval candidates and model context remain bounded: global scope does
not promise full-document reading, exhaustive enumeration or a complete per-library audit.

A global question has no "current notebook": the notebook handed to the engine is merely the first library of
the resolved scope, a naming anchor with no retrieval privilege, and EVERY citation names its owning notebook
(the first library included). Channels defined as "…for the current library" are therefore closed for the whole
run, disclosed rather than silently degraded: the notebook's hidden private Memory projection, concept roaming
(PPR), selected-source graph activation and the `index_required` call to action; the generated-question recall
supplement is off on federated legs too. In `reasoning` the closed concept roaming is also absent from the agent's
action catalog: `ppr_retrieve` leaves the reflect action enum, prompt and allow-list, and the first-round PPR seed
does not run, so the trace never shows a concept-roaming step that could only report zero passages. A model that
names the action anyway gets a skip step saying the action is not offered this run, and the loop carries on
(strict mode raises). `reasoning`'s raw-element search arm (the `search_elements` action and the automatic top-up
when every deterministic channel came back empty) is not closed but federated per library, see below. The
spreadsheet analysis arm is federated: every participant's workbooks are merged into ONE planner
catalog, planned ONCE, and up to `SPREADSHEET_ANALYSIS_MAX_TARGETS` sheets are executed, possibly from different
libraries, each its own result card (as in a single notebook); the participants are the
original-text channel's own (the same participant set, the same `CHUNK_FEDERATION_MAX_PARTICIPANTS` bound and
`CHUNK_FEDERATION_ENABLED` rollback switch), and each library contributes only visible workbooks inside the run's
frozen source ceiling. The catalog is filled library by library in rotation within the single-notebook byte
budget, so the number of workbooks read does not grow with the number of libraries, and whatever does not fit is
disclosed by count (details under "Professional Excel analysis and automatic parsing-issue archive").
Community/comparison sibling entities stay available and cover every participant;
`chunk` mode's comparison sub-queries rotate across libraries under a total cap, and single-notebook behaviour
is unchanged. Federating these channels is registered in `fangan_todo.md` pending a product decision.

The bilingual keyword recall supplement is federated instead of closed (each semantic leg already carries its
own full-text search over the sub-query text; this is the separate keyword-string arm used by `chunk` mode and by
`reasoning`'s first-round seed). It runs the single-notebook keyword search once per participant, on the same
shared executor, fair window and per-notebook budget as the semantic legs, each under that notebook's own frozen
source ceiling; a notebook with no visible source issues no query. Being a fail-open supplement, the whole arm
(preparation included) is bounded by one `GLOBAL_ASK_NOTEBOOK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` rather than the full retrieval
phase, and its timeouts never switch off a notebook's full-text search for the semantic legs. Every notebook keeps
the single-notebook recall window (`CHUNK_RECALL`); the merge interleaves the notebooks' hits round-robin in each
notebook's own keyword-score order (every notebook's first, then every second, …), keeps the first occurrence of a
passage, and stops at `GLOBAL_ASK_CANDIDATE_LIMIT`, so no notebook fills the merged list handed to the caller by
volume (`reasoning` then re-selects its seed from that list by score). A keyword leg that times out or fails only
leaves that notebook without keyword hits: it never enters the searched/skipped receipts (coverage is decided by
the semantic legs alone), and no failure of it raises a banner. The keyword passages handed on are fingerprinted
at retrieval time exactly like semantic ones, so their citations get the same recheck, without producing any
coverage receipt. Each call of the arm emits one
content-free `ask_stage` event, `stage: "global_keyword_arm"`, with participant, notebooks-with-hits, merged,
failed-notebook counts and latency. `GLOBAL_ASK_KEYWORD_ARM_ENABLED` (default `true`) is the rollback switch:
`false` closes the arm for global runs again; single-notebook asks never read it.

The exact-identifier lookup arm is federated the same way. A question that names nothing probe-worthy costs
nothing: the same zero-I/O identifier test runs first, so no participant is read, no leg is started and no event is
emitted. Otherwise the single-notebook lookup (same `EXACT_LOOKUP_*` bounds per notebook) runs once per
participant on the same fan-out and the same single per-notebook budget as the keyword arm, each notebook under
its own frozen ceiling; a notebook with no visible source issues no query. The lookup pushes that notebook's
frozen source ceiling into the probe itself, so a source outside it (a hidden Memory/Knowhow projection, or a
source added after the question was asked) neither occupies the `EXACT_LOOKUP_FTS_K` window nor takes a section
slot nor is fetched. The merge works in WHOLE SECTIONS: every notebook's first section, then every notebook's
second, …, a passage already taken is dropped, and the total stops at `GLOBAL_ASK_CANDIDATE_LIMIT` without ever
cutting a section — a section that does not fit in what is left is skipped whole and a later, smaller one may
still be taken. Every passage keeps its exact-lookup mark and its owning notebook. The reserved seats are shared
per notebook with their totals unchanged: `EXACT_SECTION_RESERVE` in `chunk` mode's `mix` selection, and
`REASONING_EXACT_RESERVE` both in `reasoning`'s single-shot synthesis prefix and in the unbound exact passages
injected into every section of per-section synthesis, are split evenly across the notebooks that returned exact
passages, in the order of each notebook's best exact passage by relevance (ties: the notebook seen first): the
remainder goes to the front, with more notebooks than seats only the first ones get one each, and a notebook with
fewer passages than its share passes the unused seats on in the same order — so one notebook's large section
cannot take every seat and no seat stays idle while another notebook still has passages. `chunk` mode's `multi`
selection likewise gives each notebook's exact passages their own quota group. With passages from one notebook —
every single-notebook ask — all of these behave exactly as before. Failures,
timeouts, receipts, banners and evidence follow the keyword arm's rules: a failed leg only leaves that notebook
without exact passages, never enters the searched/skipped receipts and never raises a banner, and the passages
handed on are fingerprinted at retrieval time. One `reasoning` `exact_lookup` action is still one lookup (now
one federated lookup) against its per-run cap. Each call of the arm emits one content-free `ask_stage` event,
`stage: "global_exact_arm"`, with participant, notebooks-with-hits, merged-passage, merged-section and
failed-notebook counts and latency. `GLOBAL_ASK_EXACT_ARM_ENABLED` (default `true`) is the rollback switch:
`false` closes the arm for global runs again; `EXACT_LOOKUP_ENABLED=false` still closes it everywhere, and
single-notebook asks never read the global switch.

`reasoning`'s raw-element search arm is federated the same way: one `search_elements` action (and the one automatic
top-up when every first-round deterministic channel came back empty) runs the single-notebook element search once
per participant, on the same fan-out and the same single per-notebook budget as the keyword arm, each notebook under
its own frozen source ceiling (intersected with its currently visible sources); a notebook with no visible source,
or outside this run's scope, issues no query, so a read-only viewer only ever gets elements they can read and that
lie inside the frozen ceiling. Every notebook keeps the single-notebook element window, and the merged **total**
is still the single-notebook element cap (8 per call), so a global search hands the model no more elements than a
single-notebook one. The merge goes in rounds: every notebook's first element, then every notebook's second, …;
within a round the elements are ordered by their own score, so when the cap falls mid-round it keeps that round's
strongest rather than the notebooks listed first (the first library is only a naming anchor and gets no positional
precedence); an element is taken once. Every element carries its owning notebook: its citation card names that
library, its `tier` is looked up for that library, and the result boundary's source check judges it against that
library's ceiling. Failures, timeouts, receipts, banners and evidence follow the keyword arm's rules: a failed or
timed-out leg only leaves that notebook without elements, never enters the searched/skipped receipts and never
raises a banner (nor does a model call that fails inside the leg, such as its query embedding: that is logged as a
`model_error` event only), and its full-text timeouts never switch off that notebook's full-text search for the semantic legs;
the elements handed to the model are fingerprinted at retrieval time from the full text that was read, so their
citations get the same recheck as every other passage. `REASONING_MAX_ELEMENT_SEARCHES` still caps the calls per
run (one federated search counts once). Within one retrieval run an element search does not repeat a passage recall
the run has already made: each library's element leg first recalls passages for its text (the `CHUNK_RECALL`
window, at least four times the element cap) and then reads elements from them, and when that library has already
been recalled for exactly that text under the same source ceiling in this run -- by the passage search (the
first-round seed, `search_chunks`, a direction's passages), by the empty-first-round top-up or by an earlier element
search -- the leg reuses that recall's ranking instead of searching again. The same holds in a single-notebook ask
whenever its element search takes the passage route (a large notebook, or a run whose ceiling binds a source list)
and in a Deep Report section's element searches; the plugin element seam passes its own source list, so it can in
practice only reuse an earlier element search of its own. A reused recall is a snapshot of an earlier moment of
the same run: when nothing is written in between, the candidates, their order and the answer are exactly what a
fresh recall gives; a source written, deleted or folded into a new scale-index generation mid-run can make a fresh
recall differ, and the reused one stays inside the run's frozen source ceiling either way. The passage search
itself never reuses anything (it needs the vectors for its diversity selection). What a run keeps is only each
recalled passage's identity, element ids and scores -- no text, no vectors -- at most
`CHUNK_FEDERATION_MAX_PARTICIPANTS` x `CHUNK_RECALL` passages and 64 recalls, least recently used out first, and
only recalls an element search could read back (a copyable notebook searched without a source list scans its
elements whole, so its recalls are not kept). A recall during which any lane failed open is not kept: a model
error, a full-text timeout or failure (the ANN-plus-full-text lane's included, whatever its banner role), a scale
index whose manifest is there but that could not be read or loaded (a torn fold rename, a file-handle or I/O error,
memory -- not a notebook that has no index), an ANN handle that did not open, a failed language or drift probe, a
failed sidecar coverage probe, and a contributor or question-index supplement that failed, timed out, was blocked,
was unavailable at run time or whose admission read failed. A contributor's availability verdict for the call
(steadily unavailable or disabled), a contributor declining the request or reporting itself disabled, and admission
rejecting its answer are not degradations: a repeat gets the same answer. A ceiling-drift flip
(a source outside the run's frozen ceiling seen on read) drops that library's recalls that were read without the
source list. `chunk` runs and Deep Report planning keep nothing. The run's closing `retrieval_run_stats` counts the
reuses as `chunk_recall_hits`, every write into the memo as `chunk_recall_stores` (a write replacing the recall
already kept under the same key included, so it is not the number held), the recalls the bound pushed out as
`chunk_recall_evictions`, and the recalls not kept because a lane failed open during them as
`chunk_recall_degraded_skips` (a run that never reuses anything shows why here). Each call of the arm emits one content-free `ask_stage` event,
`stage: "global_element_arm"`, with participant, notebooks-with-hits, merged and failed-notebook counts and latency.
`GLOBAL_ASK_ELEMENT_ARM_ENABLED` (default `true`) is the rollback switch: `false` returns global runs to the
pre-federation behaviour — `search_elements` is not in the action catalog (a model that names it anyway gets the
not-offered skip), the executor skips it too (`reason: "peer_mode"`), and the empty first round gets no automatic
top-up; single-notebook asks never read it.

**Global-run event marker**: every event written inside a global run (the `reasoning` understanding
preflight included) -- each stage's `ask_stage`, the retrieval run's closing `retrieval_run_stats`, the
per-library skip receipts and so on -- carries one extra field, `scope: "global"`. It is added in one place,
where the global run is installed (`global_ask_run`), not by each emitter remembering to. The event's own
`notebook_id` is kept as it was: in a run-level stage event it is the anchor library, in a federated leg's
event the library that leg searched, so existing consumers that read events by `notebook_id` are
unaffected; a notebook ask's events carry no such field and are byte-for-byte unchanged.
`scripts/diag_retrieval_latency.py` keeps a global run's `retrieval_run_stats` apart as
`ask_chunk(global)` / `ask_reasoning(global)` instead of adding them to the single-notebook runs of the
same kind; leaf events bucketed by library size still bucket by each leg's own library, so a global run is
neither counted twice nor filed under its anchor.

Authenticated HTTP routes live under `/api/global-ask`: `POST /ask` returns a pollable task and accepts
`replaces_job_id` ("edit and re-send": it may only name the conversation's **newest** job while that job is
`cancelled`; the row is deleted in the same transaction that inserts the new job, and a conversation that still
carries its automatic title and holds no other turn takes the new question as its title; a stale replacement is
a 409, and a retry under the same `client_request_id` replays as usual); a job echoes the
`client_request_id` it was submitted with, on the `POST /ask` response and on every later read, so a client that
lost a response recognises **its own** job in a re-read conversation — matching question text is not identity
(two browser windows can submit the same words); the public share projection never carries the field;
`POST /intent` and `POST /intent/stream` are the `reasoning` understanding preflight, taking
`{question, conversation_id?, notebook_scope?}` and returning the same understanding contract in-notebook Ask
uses. The preflight authorizes itself and resolves scope and read rights through the IDENTICAL block
submission uses; it creates no job, no conversation and no row. The streaming variant **opens the stream first** and runs
scope resolution and the authority recheck inside the heartbeat-covered work: that step re-checks read access
twice and freezes the visible source list of up to eight libraries, which takes seconds on large ones, and
doing it before the first frame means the response has sent no byte for that long — a proxy or gateway with a
short first-byte or idle timeout drops the connection and the browser can only report that understanding did
not complete (the in-notebook preflight sends its first frame within milliseconds and heartbeats every 5
seconds after that). Refusals are not lost: a 4xx written for the user with `user_error()` travels in the
`error` frame as `status` + `message` (the full Chinese sentence and the real status), any other failure stays
a content-free stable code and is logged server-side by exception **class name**; a client that wants real
HTTP status codes uses the blocking `POST /intent`. A client that disconnects cancels the understanding call.
`GET /jobs/{job_id}` reads progress or the answer.
`GET /jobs/{job_id}/stream` is the same job pushed to an attached client as NDJSON
(`application/x-ndjson`), an accelerator over that read and never a second way to run anything: it emits
`started` (always first), `progress` (the trace steps from an absolute `trace_offset` plus the CURRENT
whole coverage lists — `searched_notebook_ids`, `skipped_notebooks`, `degraded_notebook_ids` — which
replace rather than merge; the first one after `started` is a full snapshot at offset 0), then exactly one
terminal frame — `final` carrying the job as the store has it once it left `running`, or `gone` when the row
is no longer there (stopped-and-discarded, its conversation deleted, or the member's read access to one of
the job's libraries revoked mid-run); read access is re-checked **before every frame that leaves** (not at all
while nobody is watching), and a revocation ends the stream as `gone` at once, without one more step — the same
rule as polling, which authorizes each read when it is made; a follower whose own store read fails ends with
`{"event":"error","error":…}` (fixed wording, never the exception text); a service shutdown that leaves the
job `running` ends the stream with **no terminal frame** — a reader treats any of these as a lost stream and
falls back to polling — and a blank keepalive line every 5 seconds of silence. A receipt-only frame has empty
`steps` and a `trace_offset` at the end of the trace: the coverage lists are taken whether or not the trace
part of a frame fits. Authority is checked before the first frame by the same call `GET /jobs/{job_id}`
makes, so a missing or foreign job keeps its real 404. A reader applies a frame as
`trace = trace[:trace_offset] + steps` when `trace_offset <= len(trace)` and ignores a frame that would
leave a gap; re-delivery of a step it already has is therefore harmless. A client disconnect NEVER cancels
the job — it stops delivery to that client only, exactly like in-notebook Ask, and `POST /jobs/{job_id}/cancel`
stays the one cancel entry. Polling remains the fallback for a client that never opens the stream, loses it,
or sees it end without a terminal frame, and the MCP contract is unchanged: MCP follows a job by paging
`GET /jobs/{job_id}`, never through this endpoint.
`POST /jobs/{job_id}/cancel` stops execution, and
`?discard=true` means "stopped before any process output": the job **this call found running** and that then stopped (it must be
the conversation's newest; it still counts when the worker wrote `cancelled` first) is deleted together with a conversation it had just opened; a finished job, and a
job that was already stopped earlier (it may be the very record the rule keeps in the transcript), is never
discarded;
`POST /jobs/{job_id}/feedback` (body `{rating: "useful" | "not_useful"}`) records one 👍/👎 for a
finished job owned by the caller, first write wins -- a second submission on the same job does not
overwrite the first; the rating lives in that job's `payload_json` under `feedback`, never in the
in-notebook `feedback` table, so it does not surface in the notebook analytics panel or any
per-notebook feedback rollup.
`GET /jobs/{job_id}/citations/{element_id}` reads only an original element actually cited by that task.
An element flagged by the terminal citation check on any of the answer's citations or anchors is refused
with 404 and a user-displayable sentence (the refusal lives in `GlobalAskService.cited_element`, so every
drill-down shares it), while unflagged citations of the same answer still open; the flagged card keeps its
stored excerpt. The job read, the conversation detail, the push stream's terminal frame (read from the store)
and the administrator activity detail carry `citation_check` and `verification` exactly as stored; a clean
answer carries neither, and the conversation list adds no badge.
`GET /conversations` and `GET /conversations/{id}` accept `limit`/`offset`, with `has_more`/`next_offset`
on detail pages; `PATCH /conversations/{id}` renames and `DELETE` removes a conversation. Conversations
belong only to their initiating user. Browser and MCP can continue the same `conversation_id`, subject
to the token allowlist and current read rights over historical scope. Owning a conversation never widens
token capabilities. `client_request_id` supports identical retries and rejects reuse with different input.
A conversation cannot start another task while its previous answer is running.
The job's `error` is explicitly displayable Chinese retry guidance, never raw exception text.
Automatically derived conversation titles are bounded summaries; the original question remains complete.

#### After a participant notebook is deleted

When a notebook a global conversation ran over is deleted (product decision 2026-10-19), the turns that
used it stay **readable to their owner** for the retention window: question, answer body, citations and
reasoning trace are kept. The notebook-delete transaction -- the same one that writes the notebook Ask's
post-deletion projection, with the same expiry (`USER_ACTIVITY_RETENTION_DAYS`, 180 days after deletion
by default; see the deletion rule in "Admin observability: user activity" below) -- stamps
`retained_until` on every global job whose `resolved_notebook_ids` contains that library; a job that
already carries an earlier expiry keeps it, so a later deletion never extends a window an earlier one
started. Only those turns are retained and expire; the conversation's turns that did not use the library
are untouched.

- **Owner read**: for the conversation detail, a single job (stream, stop, feedback and a replay of the
  same `client_request_id` included), the owner's own activity feed and activity detail, and the
  to-do bell's "running asks", a participant that **no longer exists at all** stops taking
  part in the "every participant readable" rule -- and only for a **stamped** turn. A library that still
  exists but the owner can no longer read (removed from the group, grant revoked, deletion still in
  progress) keeps refusing the whole turn with 404: the turn may restate that library's material, and
  another library's deletion must not expose it. A turn with a missing library but no stamp (a library
  deleted before this mechanism existed, or a turn imported from elsewhere) also keeps the 404. A
  non-owner still gets 404. **Reading a retained turn over MCP / an Agent token is always 404, as
  before**: a token always carries a notebook allowlist and the deleted library left it with the
  deletion, so such a read cannot show it was ever allowed that library; retained content is readable in
  the browser only.
- **Degraded citations**: the job response gains two read-time fields that are never part of the stored
  payload: `retained_until` (when the turn is cleaned up; empty for an unstamped turn) and
  `deleted_notebook_ids` (the libraries the turn searched or cites that no longer exist). The interface
  renders those libraries' citations as a non-clickable "来源已删除" and fetches none of their images, so the
  browser sends no read request to a deleted library; every other citation stays clickable. The activity
  detail (`AskDetail`) carries the same two fields for a global turn and its pane degrades the same way. Under each such
  turn it states "本轮用到的笔记本已被删除，这一轮问答保留到 {instant}，之后自动清除。"
- **Follow-ups work as usual**: a deleted library is in no selectable scope, so a new turn never uses it and
  is never stamped; older turns that used it stay out of the follow-up context (the same rule as a narrowed
  scope). The conversation's `notebook_scope` the owner reads has the deleted libraries removed, so the
  scope the browser restores can be followed up directly; when every selected library was deleted the scope
  comes back unchanged (an empty `include` would read as "all", silently widening the user's choice) and the
  picker's existing "selected notebook unavailable" notice handles it.
- **Public sharing is not relaxed**: every open of a public link still re-checks the sharer against the
  libraries its snapshot used; a deleted library is unreadable, so a link whose snapshot used it 404s whole,
  while a link whose snapshot never used it keeps serving. Publishing or advancing a share whose range holds a
  retained turn is refused (the same 404 as a lost read right).
- **Expiry**: `retained_until` is a hard read gate against the database clock, the same rule as
  `retained_user_activity.expires_at`. An expired turn disappears at once from owner reads, the conversation
  list (a conversation every turn of which expired disappears whole), public links, the administrator's
  usage overview / activity feed / question analysis and the post-answer learning chains' samples; startup
  recovery or the next notebook deletion deletes it physically, together with any conversation it leaves
  empty. An automatic conversation title that still names an expired first turn reads as the earliest
  remaining question from the moment that turn expires -- on the conversation list, the conversation and
  the public page alike (a read-time projection) -- and the purge later writes it down; a title the user
  set is kept.

#### Global conversation sharing

A global conversation can also be published by its owner as a sign-in-free read-only page, on the
**same public page as a notebook conversation**: `/c/{token}`, read anonymously through
`GET /api/public/conversations/{token}`, with images at
`GET /api/public/conversations/{token}/assets/{alias}`. The two features are told apart by the token's
capability namespace prefix (`gshr-` is global, `cshr-` is notebook-scoped; the two namespaces
partition the token space, so neither branch ever resolves the other's token). The three authenticated
endpoints live at `/api/global-ask/conversations/{conversation_id}/share`: `POST` issues the link and
advances the watermark, `GET` reads the token/watermark back for the owner (not shared is a 404, which
is how the share dialog recognises "not shared yet"), and `DELETE` revokes (re-revoking one's own
already-unshared conversation is still 204; a foreign or missing conversation is 404 — the underlying
UPDATE is idempotent, so that 404 comes from the service's ownership gate). A global conversation
belongs to no notebook, so there is no `require_notebook_read` above these routes: ownership is the
whole gate.

The same public page has a third namespace, `alnk-`: the expiring link that MCP `ask` / `get_ask` with `delivery="link"` issue for **one answered task** (notebook or global). It is not a conversation share and never goes through the `.../share` endpoints; see "MCP answer links" under [Public conversation share guardrails](#public-conversation-share-guardrails).

Only two things genuinely differ from the notebook-scoped trio:

- **The boundary is a job**, not an answer row. `expected_through_id` carries a `job_id`; a boundary
  that does not resolve (deleted, still running, failed, cancelled, or another conversation's) and one
  that regresses behind the published watermark are both 409, with the same Chinese sentences the
  notebook-scoped route uses. A conversation with zero completed jobs is refused inside the same write
  transaction and never has a token minted and rolled back.
- **The live re-check covers a SET of libraries.** The notebook-scoped link re-authorizes the one
  notebook its conversation lives in; a global conversation lives in none, so **every open of the public
  link** re-checks the sharer's read access to the libraries this snapshot drew on — for every turn,
  the libraries it searched (`resolved_notebook_ids`) together with the libraries its evidence names
  (`cited_notebook_ids` and the `notebook_id` on each anchor and citation), always both: a turn can
  restate a library it searched without citing it, and zero citations must not mean zero re-checks.
  Losing access to any one of them 404s the
  whole link and its images, indistinguishably from an unknown token; restoring access revives the
  **same** token. The same predicate also runs at share time, over exactly the turns the page would
  serve (the page's window of the prefix ending at the boundary): a conversation referencing a library
  the sharer can no longer read on one of them cannot be published (404 with the existing
  access-changed sentence), rather than handing out a link that is dead on arrival; a turn after the
  boundary, or older than the page's window, vetoes nothing.

The personal-memory disclosure is the notebook-scoped one (see
[Public conversation share guardrails](#public-conversation-share-guardrails)) with a job as the
boundary: `GET /api/global-ask/conversations/{conversation_id}/share/disclosure?through_id=<job id>`
is owner-only, counts over the done jobs the share would publish, runs every check the share runs
(the boundary refusals and the authority sweep over the libraries the range draws on) and writes
nothing; `POST .../share` takes the same `acknowledged_memory_count` and refuses with the same 409
`share_disclosure_required`.

The share dialog's other numbers come from the server too, so a conversation of any length gets exact
numbers: `GET /api/global-ask/conversations/{conversation_id}/share/counts?through_id=<job id>&watermark_id=&watermark_at=`
(owner only, the same error mapping as the share trio, reads only). `through_id` is the boundary the
dialog asks about (empty = the newest completed job); `watermark_id` / `watermark_at` are the link's
watermark as the dialog holds it (both empty = not shared); leaving `watermark_id` out counts against
the watermark stored now, which lets the dialog ask in the same breath as it reads the share state —
the body echoes the watermark it counted against (`watermark_id` / `watermark_at`) and the dialog asks
again with its own only when they differ. The body carries `total_turns` (completed turns),
`through_id` (the boundary turn: the asked one or the newest; empty when the asked one does not
resolve), `boundary_index` (0-based; -1 when none was asked or it does not resolve —
`boundary_unresolved`), `watermark_ahead` / `ahead_count` / `boundary_omitted` / `watermark_behind` /
