  answered contributes nothing. `notebook_id` **omitted = every allowlisted
  notebook the owner can still read** (one the owner can no longer read is skipped silently, like
  `list_notebooks`), which differs from the notebook-bound tools where omitted means the default
  notebook; given, it lists only that notebook (outside the allowlist `notebook_not_allowed`,
  owner lost read access `notebook_unreadable`): its single-notebook conversations plus the
  visible global ones that used it. `limit` is clamped to 1-20; follow `next_offset` to null --
  when a page exceeds the 12,000-byte budget `next_offset` advances only past the rows actually
  delivered, so the budget never makes it skip one. Paging is by position (`offset`) over the
  newest-activity order: a conversation updated while you page moves to the front, so that pass may
  miss it or repeat one row at a page boundary -- for a complete snapshot, list again from
  `offset=0`. A negative `offset` is `invalid_argument`
  (「分页位置不能小于零，请从第一页重新读取」).
- **`get_conversation(conversation_id, turn_offset?, answer_offset?, citation_offset?)`.** Reads
  one turn per call, oldest first. A turn is one saved answer (single notebook) or one finished
  job (global: done, failed, cancelled or interrupted); a question still being answered is not a
  turn, it is appended at the end when it finishes, so the `turn_offset` of earlier turns does not
  move (a deletion or expiry shifts the later ones down -- re-read `turn_count` if needed). A page:
  `conversation` (the list row's own shape, `turn_count` included), `turn_offset` and
  `next_turn_offset`, `question`, `asked_at`, `submitted_via`, `status`
  (`answered`/`failed`/`cancelled`; always `answered` for a single notebook), `mode`, `answer` (this
  page, at most 2,000 code points) with `next_answer_offset`, `citations` (each with a `ref` for
  `read_reference`) with `next_citation_offset`, `total_citations`, `completeness_notice`, `error`
  (Chinese notice only), `scope`, `content_is_untrusted_evidence`; the number of top-level keys is
  fixed. A single-notebook turn that was asked about a deep report carries that turn's receipt in
  `scope.linked_report`, the very projection `ask` / `get_ask` build (see "Attaching a report" above: `report_id`,
  `title`, `status`, `reason?`, `sections_read`, `summary_truncated?`, `evidence_restored`, `evidence_gone`,
  `evidence_over_budget`, no Memory ids, a title cut counted in `truncation`); a turn that attached none has no such
  key. `conversation` has the list row's shape, so it also carries the `linked_report` of the conversation's last
  turn. A page carries **no** `trace`, `coverage`, `anchors` or `intent` -- for those, a job started
  over MCP still has `get_ask`. The `question` is given whole on the first page (at most 2,000 code
  points); a continuation page (`answer_offset` or `citation_offset` above 0) repeats only its first
  200 code points, ending in `…`, because the caller already has the whole question from the first
  page and repeating it would eat a large share of every page's budget; the first page is cut the
  same way only if it could not fit otherwise. Every cut counts in `truncation.omitted_characters`;
  there is no separate flag. While answer text is left, a page may carry no citations at all, and
  `next_citation_offset` then does not advance -- keep following both cursors; once the text is
  exhausted and citations remain, a page carries at least one, so every page moves some cursor.
  After the answer and citation cursors of a turn are exhausted, read the next turn with
  `turn_offset=next_turn_offset` and both other offsets at 0, until `next_turn_offset` is null. A
  conversation with no finished turn (only a question still being answered) returns a page with
  `status: "empty"`; a `turn_offset` past the last turn is `invalid_argument`
  (「turn_offset 超出这条会话的轮数（共 N 轮），请从 0 开始读取」), judged only after ownership and
  the notebook gate, so a refused caller never learns how many turns there are.
- **`submitted_via` (where it was started):** `web` / `mcp` / empty (not recorded). For a
  conversation it is the **earliest** job's origin, but empty when an answer is older than that
  job (an older conversation's first turns have no job row); for a turn it is the origin of the job
  that produced the answer, empty when no job row is found. "Earliest" is by instant, not by id or
  insertion order.
- **Who sees what (the token is re-read on every call; list and read share one rule).** The
  `read` tier is checked first -- `scope_missing` naming 「读取」 comes before any existence
  check, so a token without it cannot probe ids. A single-notebook conversation must be the
  owner's, and its notebook must be allowlisted and readable by the owner right now -- stricter
  than the browser's conversation detail, which checks only the creator, because a token is a
  standing delegation and its allowlist and the owner's access are its ceiling; the mounted
  reference libraries an answer quoted come with that notebook, and need not be on the allowlist
  themselves (the same as `get_ask` and `read_reference`). A global conversation is judged
  **whole**: every notebook that any of its unexpired turns used (per turn, the scope, the cited
  notebooks and the anchors' notebooks -- the same function the public share re-check uses) must
  be on the allowlist and readable by the owner now, and a deleted notebook counts as unreadable;
  if one fails, the whole conversation is withheld, and the list does not even show its title or
  turn count. A conversation that does not exist, is not the owner's, fails those conditions,
  has an id that does not start with `conv-`/`gconv-`, or is over 200 characters answers one and
  the same `not_found` (「没有找到这个会话（不存在、不属于此凭证的主人，或它用到的笔记本不在此凭证的白名单里、主人已无权读取）」),
  whose wording does not reveal which check failed; a dead token is `token_inactive`.
- **`list_reports(notebook_id?, limit?, offset?)`.** Lists the deep reports the owner created
  (another member's reports in a shared notebook are not listed), newest first; `notebook_id` and
  paging as in `list_conversations`. Row: `report_id`, `notebook_id`, `question` (at most 300 code
  points), `status` (`planning`/`intent_ready`/`outline_ready`/`generating`/`done`/`failed`/
  `cancelled`), `depth`, `section_count`, `created_at`, `updated_at`; no `error`, `progress` or
  `created_by`.
- **`get_report(report_id, notebook_id?, content_offset?, reference_offset?)`.** A report id
  carries no notebook, so pass the `notebook_id` `list_reports` returned (omitted = the token's
  default notebook). Only a report the owner created is readable; one that does not exist, was
  created by someone else, is not in that notebook, whose id does not start with `rep-` or is over
  200 characters answers one and the same `not_found` (「没有找到这份报告（…；请传 list_reports
  返回的 notebook_id）」), and outside the allowlist / lost access are `notebook_not_allowed` /
  `notebook_unreadable`. A page: `report_id`, `notebook_id`, `question`, `status`, `depth`,
  `created_at`, `updated_at`, the Markdown body `content` (the first page up to 6,000 characters,
  shorter when the budget requires) with `content_offset`, `next_content_offset` and
  `total_characters`, the references `references` with `next_reference_offset` and
  `total_references`, `error`, `content_is_untrusted_evidence`. The body and the references have
  independent cursors; to read only one of them, set the other cursor to its total to get an empty
  page. The first page's `question` is at most 2,000 code points; a continuation page (either
  cursor above 0) cuts `question` to 200 code points (ending in `…`) and adds `question_truncated`,
  because the caller already has the whole question from the first page and repeating it would eat a
  large share of every page's budget. A reference row: `key` (the number behind a `[kN]` marker in
  the body), `label`, `location_label`, `snippet`, `object_type`, `source_id`, `element_id`, `tier`,
  plus `notebook_id` when it comes from a mounted reference library and `ref` when it points at a
  source element or the owner's own Memory.
- **Memory and identifiers inside a report.** The body and the excerpts are what the web page shows
  the report's author (permissions belong to the retrieval layer, so nothing is filtered again
  here, and an excerpt an older report stored from someone else's Memory is still given);
  identifiers are stricter: a reference never carries the memory record the report engine stored
  (`memory_id`, `memory_owner_id`) or other internals such as `provenance` and `family_key`; a
  reference recorded as **another member's Memory** gets no `ref`, and its `source_id` and
  `element_id` are empty strings (the keys stay), because the projection source id of a memory is
  one-to-one with it -- the same identifier under another name. The owner's own Memory mints a
  `mem` ref and any other source element an `el` ref; `read_reference` re-runs its whole
  authorization when one is opened.
- **Failed reports and failed sections.** The old-format "（本节生成失败:<raw error>）" note in the
  body is always rewritten to a fixed neutral sentence, and a section's raw error is never given.
  The top-level `error` exists only when `status` is `failed`: a stored error that **contains
  Chinese** is given as stored (what the author sees on the web page, so it may carry a service
  name or another diagnostic fragment); one with no Chinese in it (an exception text) is replaced
  by 「这份报告没有生成完成，请在网页上重新生成」.
- **Private Memory and the call ledger.** `history:read` and `memory:read` sit in the same `read`
  tier, so a token that can call these tools can always read private Memory; reading a stored
  answer therefore does not add `get_ask`'s private-Memory replay gate. A test pins that same-tier
  invariant, and splitting the tiers must first add that gate to `get_conversation` and
  `get_report`. A single-notebook `get_conversation`, the two list calls that pass a
  `notebook_id`, and `get_report` each book one `history:read` row once every gate has passed; a
  list without `notebook_id` and a global-conversation read book nothing (there is no single
  notebook to book -- like `list_notebooks` and a `gask-` `get_ask`).

**Refs and `read_reference`.** `search` hits, every `ask`/`get_ask`/`get_conversation` citation, and
a `get_report` reference that points at a source element or the owner's own Memory carry an opaque
`ref` (`base64url(json)` without padding; not signed -- `read_reference` re-runs the original
read's full authorization on every call). `read_reference(ref, offset?)` reads the text behind it:
a source element (its own text, its location inside the document, and the document's display
title), one of the owner's Memory items, or an element cited by a global answer. It discloses
nothing beyond what an answer in the ref's notebook may already cite -- the notebook's own sources
plus the reference libraries it currently mounts; a Memory-derived source only to the Memory's
creator and only with the `read` tier; a Memory item (candidates included) only to its owner with
`read`; a global citation only while the job is the caller's, the citation belongs to it and
passed the answer's citation check. Anything else fails exactly like an unknown ref
(`not_found`); an unparseable ref is `invalid_argument`. Long text continues with `next_offset`.

**Source management.** Every tool here that names a `source_id` resolves it inside the
**target notebook only** (`notebook_id`, default the token's default notebook) — never the
mounted participant set, and never a hidden `memory`/`knowhow` projection row. That is narrower
than `read_reference`, which deliberately spans the mounted reference libraries because an
answer's citations already do.

`list_sources(notebook_id?, source_id?, offset=0, limit=20)` is the read-side inventory for the
target notebook and requires the `read` tier. It reuses the HTTP Sources panel's `list_sources_page` projection,
including its stable `(created_at, id)` order and its single visibility predicate: direct
user-visible imported sources only, excluding hidden Memory/Knowhow projection rows and
sources owned by mounted reference notebooks. Each row returns `source_id`, the canonical
display `title`, `file_name`, `source_type`, `doc_type`, a stored `summary` excerpt, parse and
KG state, `agent_created`, and `created_at`; it never returns `file_path`, raw
`error_message`, or file hashes. `limit` is capped at 20 by the shared MCP result rail. The
response carries `total_count`, the actual `offset`/`limit`, and `next_offset`; callers follow
`next_offset` until it is null. If the shared 12,000-byte response rail has to remove trailing
rows, `next_offset` is recomputed from the rows actually delivered, so pagination cannot skip
user data, and the ordinary `truncation` metadata still discloses the reduction. Passing
`source_id` instead returns that ONE source's full parsing/extraction state (the fields
listed below for the former status poll), which is how an Agent learns whether a source it just
added is ready to be asked about.

`add_source(notebook_id?, title?, content_md?, file_name?, content_base64?, url?)` adds ONE
document and takes **exactly one** of three input groups (anything else is `invalid_argument`):
(1) `content_md` (+ `title`, required) files a Markdown document from text the Agent provides:
`title` is at most 200 characters and `content_md` must be non-blank and within this deployment's
`SOURCE_UPLOAD_MAX_MB` per-source ceiling, measured on the stored UTF-8 bytes. The submitted title is
stored verbatim as the source's title; the on-disk file name is a separate, derived value --
sanitized, capped at 200 UTF-8 bytes (so the `{source_id}_` prefix and the `.md` suffix still fit a
255-byte path component) and suffixed -- and an over-long title shortens that file name only,
never the stored title. (2) `file_name` + `content_base64` (+ optional `title`) accepts exact
local-file bytes as strict standard base64 (no whitespace and no data-URI prefix), with the
original `file_name`. Its suffix admission comes directly from the backend parser registry, so it
supports the same local PDF, Markdown, DOCX, PPTX, CSV, XLSX/XLS, and Markdown-ZIP formats as
the browser. Decoded bytes must be non-empty and fit the deployment's ordinary per-source upload
ceiling; the file name must fit one 255-byte UTF-8 filesystem component and the optional title
uses the same 200-character source-title rail. A ZIP is not unpacked by the MCP layer: the raw
bytes enter the ordinary upload/dedup/background scheduler, then the built-in Markdown-bundle
parser persists its relative images exactly as a browser upload does. (3) `url` adds a
PDF by URL and refuses anything the server cannot reach or probe as a PDF. Re-adding
byte-identical content returns the existing source with `reused: true` instead of creating a
duplicate. All three respect the notebook's document limit, except that a re-add which
resolves to an existing source is still allowed at the limit — it adds no document, and
refusing it would break the idempotence above exactly where a retry needs it most. The limit
is enforced authoritatively inside the source-creation write transaction itself (the same gate
the browser's upload and URL-import endpoints use), so two concurrent creates cannot both take
a notebook's last slot; the metadata-only `/sources/import` endpoint alone keeps a pre-flight
check only. Parsing runs in the background, so poll `list_sources(source_id=...)`, which returns
`parse_status`, `status`, `element_count`, `kg_extracted` (whether the source has knowledge
objects in the graph), `kg_analyzed_empty` (analysis DID complete and this document legitimately
yielded no knowledge objects — a text-poor or image-only scan), `agent_created`, and — instead
of the raw `error_message`, which is `str(exc)` stored
verbatim and routinely carries server-side absolute paths — a derived `parse_failed` boolean
plus `parse_quality_warning`. The latter is the MinerU degradation signal: layout, formulas,
and tables may be wrong even though the source reached `extracted`, which an Agent about to
cite it needs to know. `reparse_source` re-runs parsing and extraction for one source and
refuses with `busy` while that source's parse lock is held (a bounded ~0.5-second probe, not a
wait: that lock spans two LLM calls, so a parse genuinely in flight will still be in flight a
second later).

`delete_source` is irreversible and deliberately narrow. It needs the `delete` tier, which
`manage` does not imply, **and** the row must have been added by an Agent. The
criterion is the `agent_created` boolean — the projection of the v48 `sources.agent_profile_id`
provenance column being non-NULL — so a document a person uploaded can never be removed
through this surface, no matter which tiers a token carries. The criterion is "some Agent
added this row", not "this profile did": Agent identities get rotated and revoked, and a
source left by a retired profile would otherwise be undeletable forever. Provenance is
written on the INSERT branch only, so re-uploading a person's bytes reuses their row and
leaves it user-added, and a notebook deep copy clears the column outright — every copied
source counts as user-added. The `sources` list and detail responses expose the same
`agent_created` boolean, and the browser's source list renders it as a neutral 「Agent 添加」
badge.

**Builds.** `build(target="kg"|"index", when?, notebook_id?)` starts a background build and
returns immediately. `target="kg"` (the default) triggers an incremental knowledge-graph
extraction (already-extracted sources are skipped; a previously partial source is retried;
`when` does not apply and passing it is `invalid_argument`); `target="index"` triggers a
retrieval-index rebuild with `when="now"` (default) or `when="idle"` for the next low-traffic
window. Both need the `manage` tier, are owner-only, and are polled through `get_notebook`
(default `include="status"`), which reports KG state (ready/building, pending source count,
current job stage and progress) together with retrieval-index state (exists/building/queued,
queue position, next idle window). `build` refusing with `busy` because a build is already
running for that notebook is a **queueing signal, not an error**: the notebook-scoped
single-flight guard is working, and the caller should poll `get_notebook` until it clears rather
than retry immediately. `target="index"` refuses with `forbidden` when the notebook is too small
to need an index. `get_notebook` is a pure read and any member of the notebook may call it.

Writes are owner-only across this whole surface. A token's allowlist may name a notebook its
owner merely joined as a read-only member; adding, re-parsing, deleting a source, or starting
a background build there would hand that share's read side a write it was never granted, so
those calls are refused. Reads keep the member-readable rule their HTTP twins use.

The four knowhow tools mirror the HTTP surface at `/api/agent/knowhow/...` (see
[APIs](#apis)) through the same service functions, so HTTP and MCP never drift on
response shape. `list_knowhow_tables`, `get_knowhow_discrimination`, and
`get_knowhow_row` need the `read` tier. `get_knowhow_discrimination` returns, for a
table with a row-title column (400 otherwise), every row's title plus each
procedure-kind column's `{column_id, column_name, text, code_status}` — enough for an
Agent to run its own discrimination logic and pick which fix applies. `get_knowhow_row`
returns one row's full cell text (`steps`/`items` for procedure/entity columns) plus
that row's **code attachments** in full. A code attachment is code an external Agent
already wrote for one cell's method — never generated or executed by the notebook, and
never embedded/chunked/indexed into any KG projection — whose freshness (`implemented`
/ `stale` / `none`) is derived at read time from a content hash of the cell; the
discrimination set carries only that status, never the code body, to stay small.
Reading code still only needs `read` — only writing it
(`put_knowhow_cell_code`, and the mirrored HTTP `PUT`/`DELETE .../code`; internal capability
`knowhow:code`) needs `contribute`, so a token that must read existing code before writing a new
version needs both tiers.

Unlike the source-management and build writes above, the `contribute` code write is deliberately
**not** owner-only: an Agent's write capability here is entirely tier-driven (design
doc §⑥-4), so a token whose owner joined a shared notebook as a read-only member can
still save a cell code attachment there. A code attachment is inert — never executed,
indexed, embedded, or projected into retrieval or the KG — while deleting or
re-parsing a document reaches every member's retrieval, which is why the two surfaces
carry different authority models. The divergence is a recorded decision, pinned on
both sides by `backend/tests/test_memory_mcp.py`.

**Notebook understanding (Agentic Memory P3).** `get_notebook(include="all")`
(the `read` tier; the default `include="status"` omits it) adds a `profile` that reads the same
[notebook understanding blocks](#notebook-understanding-blocks)
the web UI's "AI 对这个库的理解" panel shows: the `shared` layer (what every member sees) plus the caller's own
`mine` overlay (never another member's), each block projected down to `{label, value,
updated_at}` only — no `evidence` source ids, no `revision`, no change history, so a token
cannot use the response to probe source ids it has no other way to
read. Every value is marked `content_is_untrusted_evidence: true` and `citable: false` in the
response; it is prompt scaffolding for planning, never something to cite. When
`AGENT_PROFILE_ENABLED` is off, the profile reads `enabled: false` with empty blocks rather than
erroring; a notebook with no consolidated understanding yet reads `enabled: true` with empty
lists. `add_observation`
(the `contribute` tier) appends one short line — at most
`AGENT_OBSERVATION_TEXT_MAX_CHARS` (500) characters — to the caller's own observation log for
this notebook, deduplicated per `client_request_id` the same way `propose_memory` is. The
idempotency window is **bounded by ring retention** (a registered contract, not a defect):
once `AGENT_OBSERVATION_RING_MAX` newer observations have evicted a row, retrying its old
`client_request_id` writes a fresh row — an everlasting key table is not worth a migration
for a retry contract measured in seconds. It
returns immediately; the write itself is a bounded insert plus a bounded ring-eviction delete
in one transaction, with zero model calls, so there is no async status to poll. It is the
**second** Agent write that bypasses `_writable_notebook`'s owner-only gate — the first is
`put_knowhow_cell_code` — because its blast radius is structurally capped at the token
holder's own overlay rather than the whole notebook's retrieval, so a read-only member's own
Agent can still use it; see [Notebook understanding blocks](#notebook-understanding-blocks)
for what an observation is and is not used for. When the feature is off, `add_observation`
fails with `unavailable` rather than silently accepting data no consolidation job will ever read.

Only a `confirmed` Memory can be proposed for KG promotion. The creator proposes it; the
admin queue shows sanitized extraction candidates and server-validated evidence, not a raw
Memory revision/provenance browser. The proposal pins the exact source revision, sanitized
candidate snapshot, and validated evidence shown to the reviewer. Editing or deprecating a
proposed Memory atomically supersedes that proposal and resets its promotion state; edits can
then be re-proposed. The current provenance clears the proposal pointer; the pinned proposal remains
only in snapshot and queue history. Approval revalidates the Memory's current confirmed status and creator access,
plus the pinned revision and notebook binding, in the write transaction before reusing KG dedupe/merge to create or merge one
or more Base KG objects. Approval/rejection records the authenticated admin reviewer; the API
and promotion audit record the complete `base_object_ids` result. This does not change or
expose the private Memory row. A proposal whose Memory is hard-deleted is withdrawn in the
same transaction: it becomes `rejected` with reason `withdrawn_memory_deleted` and no
reviewer (a withdrawal is not a review); an already approved promotion is independent of the
Memory and stays.
A knowledge object or relation promoted into a public library is shown from the evidence snapshot stored with
it: citation cards, answer anchors, derived-chain anchors, prompts, report references and the concept panel show
the stored excerpt and title, never the current element text or source name from the promoter's private
library, and such a citation carries no link, image or table jump into that library, and the same holds for
evidence that names another library's element even under this library's source.
Since PR-E8 an approval no longer leaves the promoted evidence pointing into the promoter's notebook: the public
library gets its own provenance (`app/domain/promotion_provenance.py`). For every original — the promoter's source, or
for a Memory promotion the Memory itself — the library holds one synthetic source of type `promotion`, titled
「收录自：<original title>」 (a Memory promotion 「收录自个人记忆：<Memory title>」; approving publishes that title, by
design), reused by every later promotion from the same original. Sources written before the 2026-10-19 wording ruling
are stored as 「晋升自：…」 / 「晋升自个人记忆：…」 and are never rewritten: every surface that names a source (source
list and detail, the notebook search box, the activity feed, the share preview, MCP source output) maps that leading
prefix when it reads, through the one mapping `presented_source_title` in `app/domain/promotion_source.py`, and only
for a source of type `promotion` (or with a promotion source id) — an uploaded document that happens to be titled that
way keeps its title, and a body that mentions 「晋升」 is never touched. A title search (the sources list filter
and both legs of the notebook search box) also matches such a source under the current wording: when the query
contains 「收」 or 「录」 — the only characters that tell the two spellings apart — one more branch matches the mapped
title, for promotion sources only; every other query keeps its SQL and plan unchanged. Each evidence entry becomes one element of it. For a
generic promotion its text is the original element's current text read in the approving transaction, otherwise the
entry's stored excerpt; a Memory promotion's cards keep only the excerpt the member approved, never the element's live
text. An entry whose original is a member's Memory source is dropped (M1, fail closed), an entry with no text is
dropped, and an object left without evidence is then left out by every source ceiling. The entry points at the
library's source and element; the original source id and notebook stay on it only as `origin_source_id` /
`origin_notebook_id` display keys. Merging into an existing public object rewrites only the incoming entries, and the
reverse index follows the new sources. Because a promotion source is an ordinary visible source of the library, a
notebook that mounts the library (whose ceiling opens only the library's visible sources) and a global ask both recall
and cite the promoted object, its citation card names the original title and opens the library's 「收录自」 source, and
deleting the promoter's private notebook changes nothing. In the source detail its type reads 「收录」; in the source
list its badge reads 「已收录」 while some object's evidence still cites it, and 「不在图谱中」 once none does (for
example after the knowledge graph was deleted or fully re-analysed: a promotion source is never re-analysed, so a
curator re-promotes instead). Its `parse_status` is the terminal `extracted`, and the frontend never treats it as
still processing (it is not polled and not counted as parsing). It does not take one of the owner's uploaded-document
slots: the source list's `total_count` still counts it, while `visible_document_count` (present on an unfiltered
page only, `null` when `q` filters it) counts uploaded documents only and is what the upload gate and the 「文档 X /
上限」 indicator read. It can be deleted: its entries are removed from the evidence of every object citing it, and only an
object left with no evidence is deleted — a native object a promotion was merged into keeps its own evidence and stays;
the delete confirmation says so. It cannot be re-parsed (`POST /api/sources/{source_id}/parse` answers 409
「这份来源是收录到公共知识库的内容，不能重新解析。」, the batch `…/sources/reparse` skips it, the MCP `reparse_source`
refuses it), and no document pipeline processes it: KG extraction refuses it at its single entry (so the offline
re-extraction and `extract_source` cannot clear its objects), and it is never a KG analysis or re-extraction target,
never counted as pending analysis, never asked for paper metadata, never chunked or put in an indexing-pipeline source
snapshot, never given element vectors, image or source-fact backfills, never reported by the missing-chunks
checkup, never read by the command catalog (its routes answer 404 and the source detail shows no entry), and never
counted in the library profile's corpus statistics. An approval racing the deletion of the same promotion source waits for the deletion and writes the source
again. Data approved before the upgrade is rewritten by the PostgreSQL `0068` / SQLite v88 migration (see Operations).
Deleting a notebook eventually deletes all members' private Memory bound to it, so the delete
dialog warns about that lifecycle consequence without exposing member identities or counts; the
deletion first holds the notebook for one day so readers can take their Memory out (see
[Deleting a whole notebook: the one-day window](#deleting-a-whole-notebook-the-one-day-window)).

Hard-deleting a Memory — `DELETE /memories/{id}`, or `POST /memories/bulk-delete` with at most
200 ids (only the caller's own records count) — first removes everything derived from it: the
hidden synthetic source with its elements and element vectors, and the KG objects, relations,
source-local facts, reverse-index rows extracted from it. Every concept cluster one of those
objects belongs to is removed whole — all its member rows, in every generation — because its
canonical id, name and description can carry the Memory's text on the shared members' rows; the
surviving members are unclustered until the rebuild re-clusters them, and the notebook's graph is
marked for rebuild. The merge candidates naming those clusters and the conflict candidates
referencing the Memory's objects or relations are deleted in any status, resolved ones included,
because their stored rationale can quote the Memory. A conflict decision between shared objects
only is never touched. A merge decision is keyed by cluster, so a decided merge candidate naming
a removed cluster goes too: a merge the curator rejected (or confirmed) between that cluster and a
shared one may be proposed again after the rebuild. A merge candidate that names the Memory
object's bridge id is removed only when no cluster carries that id; a live shared cluster with the
same id keeps its candidates. If a curator manually merged a Memory-derived object into another
object, the surviving object only loses the evidence that Memory contributed; it is never deleted
with the Memory (an edit that re-extracts the Memory strips the same entries before clearing its old
graph). Every other removal of a Memory's derived source does the same cleanup:
deprecating a confirmed Memory, moving it to another notebook with `POST /memories/transfer`, and
the cleanup after an extraction that finished once the Memory was no longer confirmed. Bulk
deletes write a content-free audit event (notebook, user, count).

Leaving a shared notebook deletes the leaver's own Memory there. Of the actions that end one
person's access, only that person's own exit deletes anything. Before leaving,
`GET /notebooks/{id}/membership/exit-disclosure` returns `{"memory_count": N}`, the number of the
caller's Memory items in that notebook — every status — that leaving would permanently delete now
(0 when they are not a member, or would keep reading the notebook as its owner or through a
direct, group or everyone grant). `DELETE /notebooks/{id}/membership[?acknowledged_memory_count=A]`
then claims, under the membership row lock, exactly the C items the exit deletes now, and every
outcome says what the server did, counted by the server:

- C = 0 and A absent or 0: 204; the membership ends (or was already gone); nothing is deleted.
- A ≠ C, including A > 0 when C is 0 (the caller meanwhile lost the membership, gained a grant
  or moved the items away): 409 `{"detail": {"code": "exit_disclosure_required", "memory_count": C}}`;
  nothing is deleted and the membership is unchanged.
- A = C > 0 and the exit finishes: 200 `{"deleted_memory_count": d}`, d being what this request
  deleted.
- A = C > 0, d items were deleted, but r items the caller did not acknowledge exist (saved while
  the exit ran): 409 `{"detail": {"code": "exit_incomplete", "deleted_memory_count": d,
  "memory_count": r}}`; the caller is still a member, the d are gone for good, the r remain.
- A = C > 0 and the purge failed part-way: 503 with the same `exit_incomplete` body (d may be 0);
  still a member; some Memory may already be deleted, and a retry — which starts from the
  disclosure again — continues from there.

The membership ends in one transaction with a final count, and only the membership the claim
locked (a member removed and added back meanwhile keeps the new membership). Every step commits
on its own, so an exit whose client went away still leaves a state the next disclosure reports
truthfully. Before confirming, the user can keep their Memory in two ways:
`GET /notebooks/{id}/memories/export` downloads exactly the counted items as a Markdown file
(`<notebook>-记忆-<YYYYMMDD>.md`, each with its title, kind, status — candidates marked — times,
tags, content and provenance line; an entry's unclosed code fence or comment is closed so it
cannot swallow the next). The export reads every item in one snapshot before the first byte
is sent (PostgreSQL: one read-only REPEATABLE READ transaction; SQLite: one read transaction;
statements read 200 rows at a time; the transaction lasts as long as the server's reads, never
the download), so an exit, delete or move committing meanwhile — from another tab or device —
can never cut the file short: it holds either all of those items or none of them, never a
prefix. With nothing of the caller's left in the notebook the answer is 404
`{"detail": {"code": "nothing_to_export", "memory_count": 0}}`, never an empty file; after a
finished exit the notebook is unreadable (plain 404). The snapshot is held in memory while it is
sent, so its content is capped by `MEMORY_EXPORT_MAX_BYTES` (default 256 MB): past it the read
stops and the answer is 413 `{"detail": {"code": "export_too_large", "memory_count": N,
"limit_bytes": L}}` before anything is sent; the panel says why next to the export button. The web panel also keeps 「确认退出并删除」
and the transfer disabled while its own export is running. `POST /memories/transfer` copies or moves
confirmed items into a notebook the user owns (at most 200 ids per request; other statuses are
not transferred). The exit writes a content-free audit event (notebook, user, count).

Actions that take access away never delete Memory: unsharing the notebook (which also clears its
member list), revoking a grant, or removing someone from a granted group only withdraws access.
Access is often temporary, so the Memory stays; while access is gone nobody can read it, its
owner included, and it is visible to its owner again as soon as access returns. Deleting the
whole notebook is different: after its one-day window it deletes everything in it, members' Memory
included (below).

Leaving a group (`DELETE /groups/{id}/membership`) does not delete Memory either: it removes only
the caller's one membership row in that group. Notebooks the caller read only through that group
become unreadable, and the caller's Memory in them with them (user ruling 2026-10-21: disclose
before leaving, allow exporting first, never delete). Before leaving,
`GET /groups/{id}/membership/leave-preview` returns
`{"notebook_count": N, "memory_count": M, "notebooks": [{"notebook_id", "name", "memory_count", "pending_delete", "delete_after"}]}`:
the notebooks holding the caller's own Memory that the caller reads now and would no longer read
after leaving, each with its name and the caller's Memory count (every status, as the notebook
exit disclosure and the export count them), ordered by name; N and M are that list's length and
sum, computed by the server. The measure is exactly what the leave does: the read predicate
(`access_sql.read_access_clause`) holds now and fails once that one membership row is taken out
(`read_access_after_group_exit_clause`: both `group_members` subqueries gain a `group_id` inequality).
Notebooks still readable through ownership, a notebook membership, a personal grant, an everyone
grant or **another** group are not listed; nor are ones the caller cannot read already (being
deleted, removed long ago). A notebook inside its one-day deletion window **is** listed (ruling
B12), with `pending_delete: true` and its `delete_after`: leaving would also end the caller's way to
export that Memory before the deadline, so the panel tags it 「即将删除」 and says to export first;
every other row carries `pending_delete: false`, `delete_after: null`. A notebook whose window has
already closed is not listed. It answers only the caller's own leave: a non-member gets the same 404
as an unknown group, with no system-admin bypass. It is a plain read; the leave itself takes no
acknowledgement. The web confirmation panel says 「退出后，你将看不到 N 个笔记本里你的 M 条记忆」,
lists each notebook with its own 「导出」 (reusing `GET /notebooks/{id}/memories/export`, which
exports only the caller's Memory in that notebook) and keeps 「确认退出」 disabled while an export
runs on any notebook (the export reads and read-checks every item in one snapshot before its
first byte, so a leave cannot cut the file short, but a leave landing before the export's read
makes the export fail); in-flight exports are tracked per notebook at the groups-page level, so
a cancelled and reopened panel still sees them. When M is 0 it only says no Memory will be hidden
by leaving, with no export entry. If the disclosure cannot be read the panel does not allow the
leave (as the notebook exit does not leave blind) and offers a retry; a 404 disclosure (the caller
is no longer a member, e.g. left in another tab) says 「你已经不在这个群组里了」 and refreshes the
group list. The in-flight leave and its failure are tracked per group: switching to another group
carries neither 「正在退出…」 nor the failure text over. Rejoining shows the Memory again only in
the notebooks the rejoined member can read: those still shared with the group come back; one shared
with the group's admins only (`group_admins`) comes back only to someone who rejoins as a group admin
(an invite link joins as a plain member). The export file's note line states both that leaving the
shared notebook deletes these items and that leaving a group does not.

### Deleting a whole notebook: the one-day window

Product decision 2026-10-21 (rulings B1–B12 of 2026-10-22; spec
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-notebook-delete-grace-window_zh.md`): deleting a notebook no longer
deletes it at once. The owner's `DELETE /api/notebooks/{id}` puts it into a **one-day window**
(`notebooks.status='pending_delete'`, `delete_after = now + NOTEBOOK_DELETE_GRACE_SECONDS`). From that
instant the notebook is **unavailable to everyone**, its owner included: it is gone from every list,
search, Ask scope (notebook and global), mount, share link (`/shared`, `/c`, report and global-conversation
shares answer as for a missing library), MCP / Agent token and administrator count — `pending_delete` is one
of the values `NOTEBOOK_LIVE_SQL` lists, so every read and write path treats it exactly as a notebook being
deleted. Nothing inside is touched: members, grants, mounts, share tokens and conversations stay as they
are. Maintenance already running (a KG rebuild, say) finishes normally; a question being submitted at the
moment of the delete may fail (its write finds the notebook no longer live). When
`delete_after` passes, the delete sweep's driver C moves the row to `'deleting'` and inserts its delete
job in the same transaction; the six-phase delete then runs exactly as before, retention projection and
the global-turn stamp (#931) included. A window that closed while the server was down is promoted by the
startup sweep. The window has no "delete now" (ruling B8) and its length is a constant, not a setting
(B2); every client reads the deadline from `delete_after`.

Only five entries stay open during the window, each one deliberately:

1. **Export my own Memory** — `GET /notebooks/{id}/memories/export` works for any reader of the notebook
   (owner included, ruling B4) while the window is open: the export's snapshot classifies the notebook in
   its own first statement, and the file's header gains 「这本笔记本已被所有者删除，{时刻}起其中的全部内容（包括这些记忆）将被永久删除。」.
   The deadline means "start before it": an export whose snapshot began inside the window is complete even
   if the promotion and the Memory delete commit while it pages. Once the window has closed (deadline
   passed, promoted or not) the answer is 404 `{"detail": {"code": "delete_window_closed"}}`; after phase 3
   removed the caller's membership it degrades to a plain 404. A reader who loses read access during the
   window loses the export too.
2. **Cancel** — `POST /api/notebooks/{id}/cancel-delete`, the **owner only** (ruling B1; members and
   administrators get 404; a mirror 409 `notebook_mirrored`): before `delete_after` the row returns to its
   previous status and everything comes back as it was — **except Memory a member already moved out**
   (entry 5), which stays in its new notebook. 200 with the notebook summary; a repeated cancel answers the
   same summary. After the deadline (promoted or not) 409 `{"detail": {"code": "notebook_delete_due",
   "message"}}`; a missing notebook 404. A content-free audit event `notebook_delete_cancelled` is written
   (also `notebook_delete_requested` / `notebook_delete_promoted`).
3. **Notices** — `GET /api/me/notebook-deletions` → `{"items": [{"notebook_id", "name", "delete_after",
   "is_owner", "memory_count", "transferable_count"}]}`, the windows open now that concern the caller: the
   owner, and readers holding at least one Memory there (ruling B3); oldest deadline first. `memory_count` is
   the caller's own Memory there (every status, what the export holds); `transferable_count` the part a
   transfer moves (confirmed, not proposed for promotion). The pending-actions center shows each as a
   `notebook_pending_delete` item that **counts as unread**; when the notices cannot be read the bell drops
   only these items (logged) and keeps the rest, while the notification detail, reading its own endpoint, says it
   cannot read them. Each transition (request, cancel, promotion) refreshes the owner's and every Memory
   holder's bell (fail-open); request and cancel hand that refresh to the bounded light background pool
   (`deletion-notice`) so it never holds their answer. There is no separate reminder before the deadline (B10).
4. **Explanation code** — `GET /api/notebooks/{id}` answers a reader of a notebook inside its window 404
   `{"detail": {"code": "notebook_pending_delete", "notebook_id", "name", "delete_after", "is_owner",
   "memory_count", "transferable_count"}}`; anyone else gets the plain 404. Every sub-resource keeps its
   plain 404.
5. **Move my Memory to my notebook** (ruling B9, 2026-10-22) — `POST /notebooks/{id}/memories/transfer`
   with `{"target_notebook_id", "after"?}`: moves the caller's confirmed Memory items the move rule accepts
   into a live notebook the caller owns. Always a **move** (no copy), the server picks the items,
   `extract_kg` as the Memory page's transfer defaults it; candidates and items proposed for promotion stay
   behind (the interface says 「N 条记忆无法转移，请先导出」). **One page per request**: at most 200 items in
   id order after `after` (omitted on the first page). The answer is `{"results": [...], "remaining", 
   "next_after"}` — `results` has the shape of `POST /memories/transfer` (one entry per item), `remaining`
   counts the transferable items after this page, and the client repeats with `after=next_after` until
   `remaining` is 0 (the interface shows 「已转移 X / N 条」 meanwhile). Every page re-checks the window: its
   instant is taken once when the page starts and every item re-reads with it; once the promotion has
   committed, the remaining items fail one by one with `error_code="delete_window_closed"` while the moved
   ones stay moved, and the next page is 404 `delete_window_closed`. An item the caller can no longer read
   while the window is open (their access was withdrawn) fails with `error_code="not_readable"`; an item
   whose source the notebook's own delete removed after its copy committed counts as `moved`. **One transfer
   at a time** per caller and notebook (two running together, say from two browser windows, would copy an
   item twice): a second one is 409
   `{"code": "transfer_in_progress"}` at once (a process-local claim on SQLite, a session advisory lock on
   PostgreSQL). Only inside a window: a live notebook answers 409 `notebook_not_pending_delete` (the Memory
   page's transfer covers it); an unreadable notebook or a target the caller cannot write: 404. **Moved
   Memory never returns, even if the owner cancels.**

A repeated `DELETE` during the window is 409 `{"detail": {"code": "notebook_pending_delete",
"delete_after", "message"}}` for the owner (404 for anyone else); a notebook already being deleted,
copied or imported keeps the existing 409. A group share-request approval on a notebook inside its window
answers 409 「这本笔记本已安排删除，不能再共享。」. Global Ask turns that used the notebook are unreadable for
the day and come back on cancel; after the physical delete they follow #931 (ruling B5). Administrator
counts leave it out during the window and count its retained summary afterwards (B6). The cross-environment
sync keeps exporting a source notebook inside its window, and the four window columns are target-owned: a
mirror starts outside any window and a target can never open one on a mirror (the mirror fence refuses
the delete). Deletions that do not go through the browser route keep deleting at once (B7): the sync
import's propagated deletion, the synchronous delete used by scripts and tests, offline tooling. MCP offers
no export or notice (B11).

The browser: the owner's confirmation dialog 「删除笔记本」 says the notebook becomes unavailable to everyone
at once, is kept one day and then permanently deleted with everything in it, members' own Memory included;
that Memory holders are notified and can export or move their Memory to their own notebook; that the owner
can cancel at any time and everything else comes back, but Memory already moved out does not. It still shows
no member or Memory counts; buttons 「取消」 / 「确认删除」 (「正在提交…」 while in flight); the success toast
names the deadline. The notebook list briefly shows a compact receipt with an inline 「待确认中心」 control;
after 3.5 seconds it shrinks toward the bell over 550 ms and releases its space. Reduced-motion users get
the same brief receipt without motion. Each deletion window is introduced once per signed-in page session;
ordinary refreshes and returning to the list do not replay it. Inside the bell, 「即将永久删除的笔记本」 lists each notice with its
sentence and controls whose outcome lands beside them: 「撤销删除」 (owner; 撤销中… / 已撤销 / 「删除时间已到，
已无法撤销」 / 「这本笔记本已不存在」), 「导出我的记忆（N 条）」 (导出中… / 已导出 / 导出失败 with the reason:
over the limit, window closed, nothing left) and 「转移到我的笔记本」 (first shows 「转移后这些记忆会离开这本笔记本，
即使所有者撤销删除也不会回来。」, then a picker of the caller's own notebooks and 「确认转移」; the result names
how many moved, how many did not (「仍在这本笔记本里，请先导出」) and how many were not reached; a large set goes
page by page with 「已转移 X / N 条」 beside the button — X counts only items actually moved, failures are
counted apart — one transfer at a time — a second tab gets 「另一次转移正在进行，请等它结束后再试。」 — and
「取消」 closes the panel and stops after the page in flight; if the owner cancels the deletion part-way the row
says 「所有者已撤销删除，这本笔记本已恢复，剩下的记忆留在原处。」). A notebook mounting a library that is not live
shows the edge greyed with a reason that only states what holds, for the person looking: the library's own
owner, while it is in its window, reads 「你已删除这本笔记本，撤销删除即可恢复」; anyone else (the mounting
notebook's group admins included) 「该参考库暂时不可用」; once the six-phase delete has started, everyone reads
「该参考库已被删除」. Names stay masked as before. A 202 whose `delete_after` cannot be read still reads as
「已安排删除」 (the exact time is in the notification detail, which re-reads). A row whose deadline passed on the local clock says 「删除时间已到，正在永久
删除。」 with no control and re-reads; an unreadable list says 「暂时读不到即将删除的笔记本，请稍后重试」
(fail-closed, with a retry). Clicking the bell item expands the controls inside the notification popover
without navigating away; 「返回通知」 returns to the notification list, and closing the popover releases its space.
Closing it or returning to the notification list keeps in-flight cancellation, export downloads and paged
transfers running; reopening the detail shows their current state and results.
Even after notifications are cleared, a 「查看即将删除的笔记本」 entry remains while deletions exist or their
endpoint is unavailable, preserving access to the controls and retry. Opening such a notebook (a
stale link, a bookmark) shows the explanation box 「这本笔记本已被删除」 with the same sentence and
「撤销删除」 (owner), 「导出我的记忆」, 「转移到我的笔记本」 (opens the notification detail) and 「返回笔记本列表」.

| Bound | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Window length | 86,400 s, one day (`NOTEBOOK_DELETE_GRACE_SECONDS`, a constant, not a setting) |
| Promotion latency after the deadline | up to one sweep interval (`NOTEBOOK_DELETE_SWEEP_SECONDS`, default 300) |

The committed deterministic Memory evaluation reports Recall@5, MRR, nDCG, and three
zero-tolerance counters: candidate-to-formal-plane leakage, cross-user leakage, and
cross-notebook leakage. The A/B harness compares no-Memory, KB-only, and
KB+confirmed-Memory retrieval.

### Memory in the knowledge graph

Knowledge-graph objects and relations derived from a member's Memory belong to that member
only, by structure rather than by a display filter.

**Graph building and stored artifacts.** Knowledge-graph objects and relations derived from a
member's Memory never seed or join a shared concept cluster: a Memory object is always its own
canonical, and it is left out of canonical relations, the mention bridge and co-mentions,
communities and their summaries, and the cluster-size, largest-cluster and edge-provenance
analyses. A shared notebook's persisted knowledge-graph preview, retrieval index and
source-partition companion never contain a member's Memory: no Memory-derived object or name, no
edge that only a Memory relation supports, and no node folded into a cluster that holds a Memory
member — including memories confirmed or deleted while such an index is being built. The
knowledge-graph view and the neighbour view never show a member's Memory to anyone else; an edge
that a notebook source also supports is shown and counted on that support alone.

**Passages.** Passages are a shared index and Memory is private, so a Memory-derived source is
never chunked: both the chunking service and the chunk store refuse the write (`memory sources
are not chunked`), and a refused service call emits a content-free `memory_chunk_write_refused`
event. A whole-notebook index rebuild whose publish would put a private Memory projection's
passages into the shared index is refused before anything is published: the notebook keeps its
previously published passages and the rebuild job ends `failed` with the classified reason
`indexing_pipeline_memory_source` (「索引重建已停止：待发布的内容里混入了个人记忆，记忆不会进入共享检索。请联系管理员检查。」),
with or without a KG build. The rebuild snapshot holds visible sources only, so this is a last
line of defence.

**Reads.** Knowledge-graph reads are scoped by the viewer: the knowledge list (rows, total and
evidence items), type counts, KG search, the legacy graph, the graph and neighbour views, the
notebook card's counts and `kg_ready`, the analytics card's knowledge counts and the search box's
knowledge leg never show an object or relation derived from another member's Memory, nor an
evidence item attributed to one. An object or relation is judged by the source it was extracted
from; an evidence item by the source it names and by the source its quoted element lives in. The
graph and neighbour views show the shared graph — the same for every member, and what the stored
previews hold — plus the viewer's own Memory objects read live; `limit` bounds each of the two
layers, so a graph response holds at most twice `limit` nodes. A token without the `read` tier (which carries `memory:read`) sees
no Memory-derived row, its own included, and the notebook's Memory count is 0 for it. Notebook
counts, `kg_ready` and the analytics card's knowledge counts are the shared view plus the viewer's
own Memory-derived objects. Index node/ANN counts, the share-preview size and the rebuild-time
totals (`unified_kg_status`, the analysis card's last-rebuild size; counted once when a rebuild
ends, over non-deprecated objects and relations) count the shared graph only, so no member's
Memory count can be derived from them.

Knowledge-graph store reads take the viewer: another member's Memory-derived objects and
relations are left out of the knowledge list and its total, type and board counts, `kg_ready`,
the legacy graph, the unified graph's live path and the viewer's own-Memory overlay on the shared
preview, neighbour edges, KG search (lexical candidates are filtered before their limit; ANN hits
at hydration) and the notebook search box's knowledge leg; the viewer's own are included. Without
the `memory:read` capability (a token without the `read` tier) no Memory-derived row is returned, the viewer's own included. Community summaries,
the shared duplicate groups and the edge-review ranking never include Memory-derived rows (the
owner's own duplicate groups have a route of their own, see "The owner's duplicate groups" below). The notebook list
asks which of its notebooks hold Memory once per request, not once per notebook. A cluster that may
hold a member the viewer may not read is answered by its first visible member's object id, never by
the cluster's id (`K-` plus the smallest seed of all its members, which can spell a hidden member's
name): in KG search hits, in the graph view's nodes and edges, in the neighbour view (its focus
included) and as concept detail's `canonical_id`. For the notebook's own readers only another
member's Memory can be hidden, and once the notebook is isolated no shared cluster holds Memory, so
in practice this happens while it awaits its isolated rebuild; a mounted library read by a reader who
is not its member answers every cluster this way (see "KG detail reads" below). `GET .../concepts/{id}/detail` opens such a member id: it resolves to the member's
cluster when the viewer may see that member (otherwise it answers like an unknown id). The viewer's
own Memory concept belongs to no cluster; its detail is a cluster of one (the concept itself, its
evidence and attached objects under the same viewer rule), and other members get nothing for it.

**Writes, merges and publishing.** Knowledge objects and relations derived from a member's
personal Memory belong to that member only: they never join a shared concept cluster, never appear
as a merge suggestion or conflict candidate, can be merged by hand only with another object of the
same member's Memory, and cannot be proposed through the knowledge list. Every write that addresses a knowledge object or relation by id —
`PATCH /api/notebooks/{notebook_id}/knowledge/{knowledge_id}`, `POST …/knowledge/{knowledge_id}/merge`
(both ids), `POST …/knowledge/{knowledge_id}/promote`,
`POST /api/notebooks/{notebook_id}/relations/{rel_id}/review` — answers a caller who is not the
Memory's creator exactly as it answers for an id that does not exist (404, same body); an object
whose Memory row is gone belongs to nobody. For the creator, merge checks in this order: an object
merged into itself or two different types → 400; a missing object → 404; one side from her Memory
→ 409 「由个人记忆生成的知识对象不能与共享的知识对象合并」; both sides from her Memory and every
evidence entry of both citing one of her own Memory sources in this notebook → merged like any pair
(user ruling 2026-10-21): the result keeps the target's Memory source, so it stays visible to her
alone, its evidence is the union of her Memory's entries, and the merged-away object is deprecated
in place (she can restore it with `PATCH … {"status": "approved"}`, as after any merge). Both sides
from her Memory but either one also citing anything else — an ordinary source (what a manual merge
before the isolation left behind), another member's Memory, an entry without a source id → the same
cross-class 409, because that object carries shared evidence. A site admin has no bypass: for her a
member's Memory object is someone else's (404). The merge route requires notebook read access and
authorizes along two paths (user ruling 2026-10-22). A caller with `knowledge:write` (the notebook
owner and admin-level grantees) is checked in the order above, and on a mirror still gets 409
`notebook_mirrored`. A member with read access only can merge too, but only a pair whose two sides
both come from her own Memory, whose evidence entries all cite her own Memory sources in this
notebook, and which are both approved (no other status — conflict, reviewed, ...: merging and then
restoring would lift it to approved, around the read-level `PATCH`'s approved <-> deprecated rule
below). That verdict is reached on the rows of the read that locks both objects, in the merge's
own transaction, before anything is written; every other merge she asks for — shared objects,
another member's Memory, a cross-class pair, a pair carrying shared evidence, a self-merge, two
types, a missing object, a side that is not approved — answers exactly the 404 it answered before
(`{"detail": "Notebook not found"}`, the body a notebook she cannot read gets), so she learns nothing
about whether the other object exists or what it is. On PostgreSQL her own pair can also answer the
409 「要合并的知识对象刚被修改，请稍后重试」 under a concurrent change; a request for a pair that is
not hers is refused by an unlocked read before any lock is taken, so ids that are not hers neither queue
her behind other writers nor hold them up. On a mirror the read path
does not open (the same fence as `knowledge:write`): every merge by a read-only member answers that
404. `PATCH …/knowledge/{knowledge_id}` also requires read access and splits the same way (user ruling
2026-10-22): a caller with `knowledge:write` keeps the old path; a read-only member may only change
the status, between approved and deprecated, of an object whose primary source is her own Memory and
whose evidence entries all cite her own Memory sources in this notebook (undoing or redoing her own
merge), decided on the row the store locked, before anything is written (on PostgreSQL an unlocked
read refuses first, as for the merge). Editing the content or the owner, any other status, a shared
or someone else's object, her own object carrying shared evidence, an unknown id — all answer the same
404 and write nothing. The hand status change follows #957's rule: it drops the merged-away object's
`_merged_into` and keeps the target's `_absorbs`. On a mirror this path does not open either (reader
404, writer 409). On both write routes FastAPI's request-body validation answers 422 first (a missing
`into_id`, a field of the wrong type), before every 404 / 409 above, the same for every caller and
saying nothing about any object. Once merged, deleting, moving or editing one of the
two Memories strips only that Memory's entries from the object the other Memory owns — it is never
deleted with them; an edit re-extracts the edited Memory into fresh objects of its own. Editing,
moving or deleting the Memory that owns the merge result clears the result with that Memory; just
before, every object merged directly into it is restored to approved, and so is retrievable again,
when that object is still deprecated and its own Memory still exists (user ruling 2026-10-21). An
object whose Memory is gone is not restored. The record is on the merged-away object itself: the
merge writes the target's id into a hidden payload key (`_merged_into`; every key starting with `_`
is dropped at each exit that shows, retrieves or searches a payload — graph nodes, the owner's
overlay, concept detail, the promotion queue through `visible_payload`, and the knowledge list,
retrieval and search text through their own projections; pinned by
`test_the_owner_graph_never_shows_internal_payload_keys` on both backends and the graph view's
component test), a later merge of the same object moves it to the newest target, and a
hand edit of its status or content (`PATCH`) clears it — so an object the owner deprecated by hand
is never restored, and an object is never restored twice. Merges between shared objects write
nothing. A chain restores one level per cleared result: after a1 → a2 → a3, clearing a3 restores
a2 (which still carries a1's evidence) and leaves a1 deprecated, and clearing a2 later restores
a1; clearing a2 first (itself merged away) re-points a1 at a3. If the cleared result had been
deprecated by hand, the objects merged into it only lose the record. Only merges made from this
version on are restored automatically: a merge of one's own Memory objects left from before #824
has no record and cannot be told apart from a hand deprecation, so the owner restores such an
object herself with `PATCH … {"status": "approved"}` (user ruling 2026-10-22). On PostgreSQL the
teardown locks every object it will write — its own and the objects whose evidence it strips — in
one id-ordered statement first, so two Memories merged into each other's objects and deleted at
once queue instead of deadlocking; the restore then takes the restored objects' Memory sources and
rows with `SKIP LOCKED` and never waits inside the teardown. The lock may be held by that Memory's
deletion or re-extraction, but also by relation completion, an extraction publish, an element swap
or a transaction that then rolls back, so whatever was skipped is re-run right after the commit in a
short transaction (same lock order, re-checked, harmless to repeat). That re-run runs on the
delete's or edit's own request, so its wait is bounded to a few seconds (`lock_timeout`); a lock
held longer hands the notebook to one background pass that waits longer, and whatever even that
misses — or a crash in between — is settled by a background pass after the next start. That
background pass runs in the light maintenance pool, at most one per notebook at a time in a
process; a re-run that times out while that pass runs marks the notebook, and the pass reads it again
from the start when it is done, so nothing left meanwhile is skipped. So the only window that waits
for the next start is a re-run and the background pass after it both failing, or the process being
killed between the commit and the re-run (or during the background pass). These
passes read on a read-only connection, Memory sources first and then their objects, so their cost
follows the amount of Memory, not the size of the notebook. Before restoring, a pass checks whether
another source's object still carries all of the object's own evidence (a chain link the skipped
step would have re-pointed to) and re-points it there instead, so an object is never restored as a
second copy; only an object still in use that carries the merge mark, or a deprecated chain link that
itself carries the record, qualifies as such a target (a hand-deprecated one does not, and the object
is restored), and re-pointing also marks the target. A candidate whose evidence is empty cannot be
compared and is always restored. A step that would only have dropped the record (its result had
been deprecated by hand) and that was skipped inside the transaction and not completed by the
in-request re-run either is handled by the background pass as a restore. If a re-point's target is
deleted while the step waits for its lock, the step is left as it was and the pass re-reads it: with
no other eligible holder left, the object is restored. The merge also marks its target (a hidden `_absorbs` key, kept across hand edits; a
stale mark only costs one more read): a Memory removal or edit whose objects carry no such mark
skips the follower read entirely, so with a certified reverse index a plain Memory removal pays one
statement more than before this feature. On PostgreSQL a merge locks the Memory sources it
makes the target cite before the object rows (the order of every Memory removal and re-ingest), so
a concurrent delete, member exit or edit of one of them waits for the merge and then strips what it
wrote; in the rare case that another merge put a new Memory's evidence on the source object between
those two steps, the merge answers 409 「要合并的知识对象刚被修改，请稍后重试」 and writes nothing.
A promoted Memory does not change any of this: the promotion copies into the public library and
leaves her private objects as they were, and the public copy is the library's own object (its
evidence cites the library's `promotion` source), merging there like any public object. Proposing her own such object answers 409
「由个人记忆生成的知识对象不能在这里申请贡献到公共知识库，请在你的记忆里提交」 and queues nothing; a Memory
reaches a public library only through its creator's `POST /api/memories/{memory_id}/promote`.
Nothing is written on a refusal. The upgrade migration closes open generic proposals of such
objects as rejected (reason `memory_derived_object`, no reviewer); if one is approved anyway, the
approval answers 409 「这条贡献申请指向由个人记忆生成的知识对象，已自动关闭」 and closes it as rejected,
reviewed by the approving admin. Approving a proposal whose knowledge object no longer exists
answers 409 「这条贡献申请对应的知识对象已不存在，申请已自动关闭」 and closes it as rejected (reason
`object_missing`); an unknown proposal id stays 404. The review dialog shows the reason on the item
and refreshes the queue. `POST /api/notebooks/{notebook_id}/tier` with `tier=base` answers 409
「这本笔记本里还有成员的个人记忆，不能发布为公共知识库；请先让成员转移或删除自己的记忆」 while the notebook
holds a knowledge-graph source generated from a member's Memory, and the tier is unchanged;
withdrawing a publication (`tier=personal`) is never refused. The refusal is shown next to the
publish control. Conversely a Memory-derived source is created only while the notebook is not a
public library: a Memory confirmed before the notebook is published does not reach it — its queued
analysis re-checks when it runs and ends without creating anything. With both guards, a Memory
reaches a public library only through its creator's `POST /api/memories/{memory_id}/promote`.
Checkup item H11 (read-only, `fix: none`, shown as a notice card, never rings the bell) counts the
Memory sources a public library still holds — possible only for libraries published before these
guards, or a public library received through sync import (which copies the `notebooks` row without
going through publishing). The edge review queue, the bell's edge-review count and the shared
duplicate groups (`GET …/duplicates`) leave Memory-derived rows out for everyone, the Memory's owner
included.

**The owner's duplicate groups.** `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/duplicates/own-memory?type=` answers the
caller alone with `{groups, merged_away}`. `groups`: among her own live Memory-derived objects of the
requested type, those whose evidence entries all cite her own Memory sources in this notebook (the
merge rule above, judged one object at a time, so every listed pair merges), grouped by the same
rules as the shared groups — normalized-name seed, acronym alias, similarity hint and order (larger
groups first). For a caller without `knowledge:write`, `groups` hold approved objects only (the
read-level merge accepts nothing else); a writer's groups are unchanged. `merged_away`: her objects of
the same kind that are deprecated and still carry a
merge record (`_merged_into`: deprecated by a merge and not touched by hand since), the ones she can
restore with the status `PATCH` above; hand-deprecated objects are not listed. It requires notebook
read access; another member, a site admin and a token without `memory:read` all get two empty lists
(not 404), the same answer as a caller who owns no Memory here. It is a route of its own because `/duplicates`
answers a bare list, so a field only for the owner would change its shape for every client; the
shared groups, their read and their response bytes are unchanged. Neither is cached. The owner's
groups are read by the caller's identity alone, with no notebook-wide viewer scope, in two passes shaped
like the shared read: pass 1 is one statement that reaches her own Memory sources through the partial
Memory/Knowhow source index and her objects through their source index, returns only id, status and
name (plus the payload for a procedure, whose seed reads the steps), and judges "every evidence entry
is her own Memory" in the statement; pass 2 reads payloads by id for the group members and
`merged_away` only. Both grow with her Memory in the notebook, not with the notebook. Evidence that is
not an array counts as no evidence when it is `null`, `{}` or the empty string (as the merge reads it)
and is not listed otherwise. They take no part in merge suggestions or model review.

The knowledge browser's 「查重」 shows them as a section of their own below the shared groups,
「我的记忆里的重复」, with the line 「这些条目来自你的个人记忆，只有你能看到」, expanded and paged on its
own, and absent when she has neither such a group nor anything to restore. The section ends with
「合并时弃用的条目」 (「恢复后，这一条会重新出现在你的检索结果里」), one 「恢复」 per row — the
status `PATCH` above. A read-only member gets 「查重」 too, with only that section; she never asks for
the shared `/duplicates`. In the knowledge list her deprecated objects still show their status
read-only; restoring lives in this section. Mirrors show no 「查重」. Merges and restores answer where
they happened: inside the group merged into (or the row) while it is on the current page, and at its
former place when the write took it off the list (a merge left a single member, a restore moved it
out of 「合并时弃用的条目」), clearing on their own timer, instead of a page toast: success
「已合并，原条目已弃用」 or 「已恢复」; a write that succeeded while the section could not be read
again 「已保存，但这一段没能刷新，请重新点「查重」」; a 409 shows the server's words and reloads that
section; a 404 shows 「这条已不在了」 and reloads that section. While a write runs its button reads
「合并中…」 / 「恢复中…」 and every button of both sections is disabled. A section that could not be
read says so in its place (「…没能读取：<reason>」) instead of 「未发现重复。」.

**Checkup.** `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/checkup` also lists four read-only items: H9 (the notebook's
knowledge graph awaits the one-time background check and rebuild after the upgrade), H10 (approved
generic promotions of Memory-derived objects), H11 (Memory sources a public library still holds,
above) and H12 (ownerless Memory sources, above). All four are read-only (`fix: "none"`), shown as
notice cards without a button, never counted in `healthy`, and never raise the bell. The upgrade
and its completion check are described in
[Operations: Memory isolation in the knowledge graph](./operations.md#memory-isolation-in-the-knowledge-graph).

## KG extraction trigger

- Built-in relations share one directed endpoint contract across extraction and graph consumers. Historical rows that violate a core-type pair remain auditable but cannot affect graph/PPR/canonical/relation retrieval. Administrator-defined object types remain extensible for known edge ids. Optional cross-element completion advances bounded source-generation keyset pages using indexed same-source candidates, is double-verified, rollout-gated, and disabled by default; it never performs document- or book-wide full scans.

- Edge trust & curation: per-edge trust signals (evidence / corroboration / type-validity) plus a curator review queue; reviewer-rejected edges are excluded from graph reasoning

- Knowledge governance: browse by type via `/knowledge-types` + `/knowledge?type=...`, status lifecycle, duplicate detection & merge, conflict detection; `deprecated` objects excluded from retrieval and 1-hop expansion. Personal→base node promotion (propose → under review → approve/reject) with dedup-on-approve and a curator promotion queue

Chunk-native retrieval is ready as soon as a source is parsed + embedded, so **KG extraction is opt-in per notebook** rather than run on every upload:

| Notebook state on upload | KG extraction | How it happens |
|---|---|---|
| No KG yet (fresh notebook) | **Not** auto-run | Build on demand: `POST /api/notebooks/{id}/kg/build` (UI: a notebook's **构建知识图谱 / Build KG** action; also surfaced when you pick the **深入分析** group — the `strict` mode `reasoning` — on a KG-less notebook) |
| Already has a KG | **Auto-run** in the background for each new source | No manual trigger — keeps the KG complete; the new source is then incrementally fused into the unified cross-document KG |

The ingest-time decision is `KG_AUTO_EXTRACT or notebook-already-has-KG`:

- `KG_AUTO_EXTRACT` (default `false`) — when `true`, every upload extracts KG for **all** notebooks.
- Otherwise extraction runs on upload only if the notebook already contains KG objects.

So you **opt in once** (build the KG, or set `KG_AUTO_EXTRACT=true`); after that, new documents are auto-extracted and fused. Re-extract a whole notebook from scratch with `POST /api/notebooks/{id}/kg/rebuild`. For bulk/offline builds, see [Offline batch ingestion](./operations.md#offline-batch-ingestion-directory--kg).

All model-backed KG passes—initial extraction, gleaning, and refinement—default
to `thinking.type=disabled` through the OpenAI-compatible `extra_body`, without
inspecting the bound model name. Their outputs are structured facts, not
reasoning traces, so hidden thinking is neither read nor stored. Deployments may
override those workload defaults in `[thinking]`; the KG availability probe is
the exception and always forces thinking off. This policy does not alter Ask,
Report, or any non-KG workload.

### KG build failure isolation

Manual notebook builds/rebuilds create a durable, task-scoped `kg_build_jobs`
row and allow only one running KG task per notebook. The notebook and index
status APIs expose `probing → extracting → stopping → finished`, source counts,
and a safe user-facing failure message; the frontend shows the same state after
refresh and offers **继续分析未完成内容** after a failure.

The build **total is accurate at start, not at acceptance**. Accepting a build no
longer enumerates the whole library on the request path, so the row is created
with `total_sources = 0` and the `kg_build_started` event always carries `0`. The
worker counts its own targets with exactly the predicate and limits it will then
iterate — for a rebuild that clears existing data, *after* the delete phase, so
the count and the extraction loop see one world — and backfills the durable total
before it switches the stage to `extracting`. While the run is
**running**, a `total` of `0` on `get_notebook` is only visible during the
`probing` stage, which the browser renders as 「正在连接模型服务…」 without any
numbers. A **terminal** row can also carry `total = 0`: either the run truly had
no targets, or it failed/was interrupted before ever reaching the counting point
(a failed startup probe on a rebuild, a crash settled by startup recovery) — an
interrupted card can therefore read 0/0 where it used to show 0/N.
The total may still rise once more mid-run: the late-arrival backfill rounds add
sources that landed after the count, and the same monotonic rule applies (a
denominator never moves backwards).

An interrupted task settles into that same failed state: a Ctrl-C or termination
signal on an offline batch run stops in-flight windows cooperatively, drains them
before the task settles (the guard is released with that row), and records
`worker_interrupted`, so a killed run never leaves a notebook displaying an
analysis that never finishes. Only an uncatchable end (SIGKILL, OOM kill, power
loss) leaves the row in progress, and that case is settled by startup recovery.

Each KG model request uses `KG_LLM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (default `60`) and at most
`KG_LLM_MAX_RETRIES` retries (default `2`, allowed `0..3`). KG requests ride
the streaming transport, so that timeout bounds the connect phase and each wait
between streamed chunks rather than the whole reply: a long extraction that
keeps producing tokens is not cut off at 60 seconds, only a silent upstream is. If transient
unavailability persists, or the service rejects/authenticates the request
permanently, the shared control for that one job stops new requests, cancels
queued source/window work, publishes `stopping` from the first failing window
before either window- or source-level draining, and then drains calls already
in flight. Probe and extraction calls forward that control's cancellation signal
to the shared streaming JSON transport. The timeout therefore guards inactivity
between received chunks (and initial response latency), rather than imposing a
wall-clock cap on a long completion that continues to make progress; a gateway
that buffers the stream or enforces its own hard request deadline remains outside
this guarantee. The transport requests the optional OpenAI-compatible usage
trailer and records exact prompt, completion, and total token counts from its
final empty-choice chunk in the existing per-user LLM log. A provider that
explicitly rejects that option falls back to ordinary streaming; the physical
client remembers the rejection so later calls do not repeat it. If a provider
accepts or ignores the option but emits no usage, the log leaves token counts
unavailable rather than estimating them locally. Other notebooks and later tasks
are unaffected. The availability
probe explicitly bypasses the LLM response cache and does not populate it, so a
stale successful probe cannot authorize destructive rebuild work during a live
outage. It reuses the configured short-output budget instead of imposing a
smaller probe-only cap, because reasoning-capable providers may consume a tiny
cap before emitting visible JSON. An HTTP-success response with empty,
truncated, or otherwise invalid JSON is recorded as `model_response_invalid`;
the UI identifies it as an unusable model response rather than an operator
interruption and preserves the retry action.

**Offline skip mode (opt-in, CLI only).** Stopping the whole task is the right
default for an interactive build, but it is the wrong trade for an unattended
run over thousands of sources: a single flaky window kills a multi-hour batch.
`scripts/batch_ingest.py kg --skip-model-failures` narrows the blast radius of
"model unavailable" from the task to **one source**. That source gets its own
child of the run control, so only its own in-flight windows are cancelled and
