Mounted consumers stop retrieving deleted knowledge. After graph commits, the preview is republished for retained hidden objects within budget or retired when empty/over budget. Preview failure or a held claim is fail-open and can leave stale preview until a later refresh/index build.

  Delete additionally checks for another process's running `kg_build_jobs` row immediately after claiming; a later external job is outside that one-time check. It never sets the build marker (`kg_building` still means extraction). Before draining, it marks finished build rows `stage='cleared'`, retains those rows for usage counts and leaves running rows alone. A cleared latest row projects as `kg_build: null`, even after partial deletion failure; the next analysis reports normally. Errors remain internal; events are `kg_deleted` (counts) or `kg_delete_failed`. Notebook deletion waits for a running KG delete, while a notebook-delete tombstone stops the KG job. KG deletion uses the heavy maintenance queue, separately from the notebook-delete queue.

  Incremental `POST .../kg/build` finishes with at most three backfill rounds for sources whose elements arrived behind its cursor, never beyond `target_limit`. Remaining unattempted sources produce `status=succeeded`, `error_code="kg_backfill_partial"`: the next incremental build continues.
- `GET .../concepts/{canonical_id}/detail?limit=&after=` — concept detail keyset-paginates the hub cluster's members (`limit` defaults to and is capped at 200; `after` is the `id` of the last member on the previous page). The response adds `member_total` (same predicate as the page query, deprecated members excluded) and `next_cursor` (the last member `id` on this page when a further page remains, otherwise empty). `member_total` is only recomputed on the first page (`after` empty) — a hub cluster's COUNT is the same order of cost as the whole-cluster read this pagination replaced, so re-running it on every "load more" page would repay most of the savings; every later page answers `member_total: null`, and the browser carries the first page's total forward instead of re-fetching it. `attached` and `evidence` moved from whole-cluster to **per-page-member** scope — each page reports only the adjacency and evidence of the members it just returned; paging through every page still surfaces the complete set, so this is pagination, not truncation (a handful of concepts have hub clusters with thousands of members, which this endpoint used to return in one shot together with every member's full payload/evidence). This detail is consumed only by the graph view's detail panel ("load more members"); it never feeds the unified-graph render itself. `GET .../objects/{object_id}/context` — object detail for the graph panel and the knowledge browser: `{id, object_type, name, section_path, occurrences, definition, definition_basis, definition_source_id, definition_element_id, steps}`. `definition_basis` names where `definition` came from — `cluster_description` (the concept cluster's fused description), `defines_evidence` (the element text of a `defines` relation's evidence, located by `definition_source_id` / `definition_element_id`), or `defines_name` (a definer's name when it has no evidence; never returned under a source ceiling) — and is `null`, together with `definition` and both locators, when there is none.
- **KG detail reads apply the viewer's readable sources.** In a notebook the viewer is a member of, those are the notebook's visible sources plus the viewer's own hidden sources (Knowhow projections, and Memory the viewer created); in a mounted library the viewer is not a member of, that library's visible sources only. Three reads apply the rule to objects — object context, concept detail, and neighbour hydration (`GET .../objects/{object_id}/neighbors`): an object is hidden from the viewer when its own source (the one it was extracted from) is a hidden source the viewer may not read, whatever its evidence cites, or when its evidence cites such a source and nothing the viewer may read. Object context hands the store the readable set as its source ceiling, so the fused description is dropped when any cluster member cites or was created from an unreadable source, and unreadable `defines` evidence, occurrences, steps (legacy sibling steps are judged on the sibling's own source too) and the section path are dropped by the same predicate; a hidden object answers **404**. Concept detail omits hidden objects from `members` (a page still carries `limit` visible members when they exist, and `next_cursor` is the last visible one) and from `attached`, drops unreadable items — an item is readable only when both the source it names and the source its element lives in are — from each member's `evidence`, from each attached object's `evidence` and from `evidence`, answers 404 when the cluster has no visible live member, and labels a cluster that may hold hidden members — some member is created from or cites an unreadable source — with its first visible member's name (member-id order). `member_total` excludes hidden members: exactly when the first page read the whole cluster, otherwise the members hidden by their own source plus those the page scan met. Neighbour hydration judges every node on its own identity — a raw object by the object rule, a folded cluster by its members — so it omits hidden objects, clusters with no visible live member (including clusters no member of which is created from an unreadable source but every member of which cites only one), and the edges touching them, relabels clusters that may hold hidden members the same way, fills `cap` with visible neighbours, and answers a hidden focus exactly as it answers an unknown id (its `source_notebook_id` echoes the requested library, or the active notebook when none was given, as for an unknown id), deciding that before it reads the neighbourhood. These reads do not filter edges between visible clusters, their `edge_type`, or `support_count` / `source_count`, nor the unified graph (which also supplies the panel's node title), KG search, pending merges or conflicts (only the side names of a pending merge take the cluster label rule, see `GET .../unified-kg/pending-merges` above), or analysis. Those surfaces are read only by the notebook's own readers, who may read its Knowhow projections, and once the notebook is isolated no shared cluster holds Memory, so the canonical ids and stored names they return (the pending merges' `canonical_a` / `canonical_b`, the analysis' `largest_clusters`, the findings' `canonical_ids`) spell no member those readers may not read. When no hidden source of the notebook is unreadable to the viewer, and the viewer is not reading a mounted library they are not a member of (below), nothing is filtered and every response is byte-identical to the unfiltered one; deciding that takes two reads bounded by the notebook's Memory and Knowhow count (`memory_source_ids` and `hidden_source_ids`), plus one access check for a mounted library. A filtered read then reads the notebook's visible sources once; concept detail and neighbours add one statement, whatever the number of such sources, that returns the objects owned by unreadable sources, the objects citing them through the reverse evidence index, and whether that index is certified complete, plus one statement per 900 of those objects to find their clusters; a neighbour read adds one batched statement for the first members (at most 8 each) of every returned cluster that may hold a hidden member, and pages through a cluster on its own only when none of its first members is visible. When the reverse index is not certified complete for the notebook, every cluster is treated as possibly holding a hidden member. **Through a mount, a reader who is not the library's member never gets a merged object's own id or stored name.** Concept detail and the neighbour view of such a read apply the viewer rule even to a library with no hidden source, and answer every cluster — not only one with a live hidden member — by its first visible member (member-id order): that member's object id as node id, edge endpoint, `focus_id` and `canonical_id`, and that member's name. This also covers a name a pruned member left behind (a Knowhow re-projection or table delete keeps the cluster's stored id and name until the library is merged again). The same prune clears the fused description of every cluster that lost a member, in the same transaction — it was written from every member's quotes — so object context and Ask anchors fall back to `defines` evidence for that cluster until the next merge writes it again. A cluster id given as input answers exactly as an unknown id: concept detail answers the same 404 for every id that does not open a visible member's cluster (an unknown id, a cluster id, a hidden member, an unclustered object), and a neighbour focus that is not a raw object gets the unknown id's neighbourhood; a member id opens the member's cluster as above. The library's own members reading through the same mount see cluster ids and names unchanged. Cost: on top of the two bounded reads the non-member rule already makes, a neighbour read adds one primary-key identity read of the response's ids (it tells raw objects from cluster ids) and one batched read of the first members of its clusters (a window of one when the library has no hidden source); concept detail takes the label and the answer id from the page it already read. The browser treats a detail 404 as "nothing to show" (no error banner; a "load more members" 404 ends paging with the line 「没有更多可显示的成员」) and renders no definition row when `definition` is empty.
- KG quality-analysis report reads (notebook-read gated): `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/kg-analysis` — optional `boards`/`top_members`/`edges` limits, returns object composition, per-object-type convergence, the topic-community list, and cross-community edges, each stamped with the `kg_mutation_seq` it was built at; `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/kg-analysis/sources` — optional `limit`/`offset`/`order=sparse|connected`, paginates per-source profiles. Both only read the `kg_community_edges` / `kg_source_profiles` / `kg_analysis_artifacts` precompute product tables written by `unified-kg/rebuild`. The overview also returns `findings_summary` (the findings ledger row and the marks only: freshness, per-rule status, counts, the S1 development item, structure, comparison, the relink mark with `may_change`) and `merge_code`. `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/kg-analysis/findings` — `zone=open|passed|dismissed`, `limit` ≤ `KG_FINDINGS_PAGE_MAX=200`, `offset`; one page of findings in one read snapshot, not memoized; every row carries the read-side `status` (`open`, `handled` with a `handled_reason`, `dismissed`, `decided_not_same`, `relink_spent`) and `live_sources` (each referenced source's existence, title, type and whether it is processing, by primary key, at most one page). Row evidence carries only counts, visible sources' ids and titles, canonical ids and names read from visible sources' own objects; the v1 seeds F4 stores for every member to match stored merge decisions are matching keys, used server-side only and never returned (the findings' readers are the notebook's own, who may read every member a shared cluster holds; see "KG detail reads"). `open` holds open and handled rows, `passed` the F4 groups the user decided apart and an exhausted F5, `dismissed` the rows marked as normal. `PUT` / `DELETE /api/notebooks/{id}/kg-analysis/findings/{rule_id}/{subject_key}/dismissal` — mark as normal / undo; requires `kg:write` (the level of merge confirmation), 409 on a mirrored notebook, 404 without access; PUT is 404 unless the key is in the current findings, DELETE is idempotent; both return 204. Dismissals outlive the findings and accumulate; once the notebook's marks reach `KG_ANALYSIS_MARKS_MAX`, a new dismissal returns 409 with a displayable message (undo some first) and no existing mark is touched; the overview's `counts.dismissed` counts only dismissals whose subject is in the current findings. The editor-only in-panel generate/update control calls the existing `POST /api/notebooks/{id}/unified-kg/rebuild`; it is not an analysis endpoint of its own.
- Global graph-type baseline (admin writes): `GET /api/object-schemas`, `POST /api/object-schemas`, `PATCH /api/object-schemas/{type}`, `DELETE /api/object-schemas/{type}`.
- Notebook-effective graph types: `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/object-schemas` requires notebook read access; `POST /api/notebooks/{id}/object-schemas`, `PATCH /api/notebooks/{id}/object-schemas/{type}`, and `DELETE /api/notebooks/{id}/object-schemas/{type}` require notebook owner access. Patching an inherited global type creates a notebook override. Deleting an override restores inheritance; deleting a notebook-only type removes it only when no knowledge object of that type remains. `POST /api/notebooks/{id}/schema-proposals` stores review-only proposed types in that notebook rather than the global baseline; a proposal never suppresses an inherited type until the owner explicitly activates it. Global and notebook writes are serialized across both registries and proposal results are rechecked after the model call. Database merge preflight rejects same-name global definitions whose semantic columns differ rather than silently keeping the destination row. `object_type` and every field key must start with a lowercase ASCII letter, contain only lowercase ASCII letters, digits, and underscores, and contain at most 80 characters. A definition may contain at most 64 unique fields and 64 unique list fields; `primary` must be one of `fields`, and every list field must also be in `fields`. Each human-facing schema text value (`plural`, `label`, `description`, and proposal `rationale`) is limited to 2,000 characters. The browser applies the same creation/editing rails before submission; the API remains authoritative.
- `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/duplicates`, `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/duplicates/own-memory` (the owner's own groups), `POST /api/notebooks/{id}/knowledge/{knowledge_id}/merge` (read access; a read-only member merges only two of her own Memory objects, see "Memory in the knowledge graph")
- Two-tier: `POST /api/notebooks/{id}/tier` body `{tier: "base" | "personal"}` → returns the updated `NotebookSummary` (400 on bad tier, 404 on missing notebook). Sets the notebook's federation tier (base = publishable as a public knowledge base, personal = default user notes); a `base` notebook only participates in another notebook's retrieval once that notebook explicitly mounts it (`GET`/`PUT /api/notebooks/{id}/bases`, candidates via `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/mountable`).
- Reference-library mounts: `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/bases` → `MountedBase[]` (this notebook's mount edges, including greyed-out inactive ones); `PUT /api/notebooks/{id}/bases` body `{base_notebook_ids}` → full replace, returns the updated `MountedBase[]` (400 if any id is outside the mountable candidate set; owner-only); `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/mountable` → `MountableNotebook[]` (mountable candidates: every public knowledge base, this notebook's own same-owner libraries, and — since group knowledge sharing — every library this notebook's owner can read, subject to the borrowed-mount gate; each candidate carries `origin ∈ {base, mine, shared}` so the picker can group them truthfully).
- Group, membership, invitation and notebook-grant routes: [Group sharing endpoints](#endpoints); authorization and lifecycle rules are defined in the same chapter.
- Edge trust & curation: `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/edge-review-queue` → `{items: EdgeReviewItem[], total}` (edges ranked by review priority desc, `limit`-bounded — default 100; `total` is the queue's true size, independent of `limit`, so the UI can show the full remaining count instead of just the page it received — it is the non-rejected edge count belonging to the SAME version as `items`, always read together from one seq-gated ranking memo so the two numbers can never describe two different KG snapshots), `POST /api/notebooks/{id}/relations/{rel_id}/review`
- Governance / promotion: `POST /api/notebooks/{id}/knowledge/{knowledge_id}/promote`, `GET /api/promotion-queue`, `POST /api/promotion-queue/{candidate_id}/approve|reject` — both `promote` routes (knowledge and `POST /api/memories/{memory_id}/promote`) accept an optional `target_base_id`: with one mounted public library it defaults to it; with several it must be given; a notebook with no mounted public library, or a target outside its mounted set, is rejected with `400`. Approval reads the stored target; legacy candidates without one cannot be approved until `scripts/backfill_promotion_targets.py` assigns it (the queue greys out their approve button).
- Deep Report routes under `/api/notebooks/{id}` follow the [lifecycle and execution rails](#deep-report-lifecycle-and-execution-limits):
  - `POST /reports` accepts `{question, depth?, auto_generate?}` and returns `{report_id}`; `GET /reports/{rid}` returns durable understanding, status/progress, outline, `content_md` and live `section_status`. Each outline section carries `intent_ids`, `intent_questions`, editable `sub_queries`, and objective `coverage`, alongside perspectives, tensions and sufficiency.
  - `POST /reports/{rid}/intent` accepts `{resolved_question, answers:[{id,answer}]}`; successful atomic confirmation returns `{status:"planning"}`, duplicate/stale confirmation returns 409. Planning stops at `outline_ready` unless the original request selected automatic generation.
  - `PATCH /reports/{rid}/outline` accepts `{sections}` only in `outline_ready`, preserves the server intent catalog, and returns 422 for no valid section, loss of a mandatory intent's last section, or excess sections/directions. `REPORT_MAX_SECTIONS` and `REPORT_MAX_SUBQUERIES_PER_SECTION` also gate the browser through `/api/system/config`; input is never silently truncated.
  - `POST /reports/{rid}/generate` accepts `{depth?}` only from `outline_ready` or a failed report retaining its outline (otherwise 409). Retry keeps confirmed intent/outline and clears generated artifacts atomically.
  - `GET /reports`, `POST /reports/{rid}/cancel`, and `DELETE /reports/{rid}` list, cancel and delete.
  - `GET /reports/{rid}/followup` returns the retrieval scope 「就此追问」 switches to (the scope the report was generated under, minus what no longer exists); another member's report 404, an unfinished one 409, see [Follow-up questions on a deep report](#follow-up-questions-on-a-deep-report).
  - `POST /reports/export` accepts `{report_ids}` and returns `reports.zip`, selecting completed nonempty reports by notebook and creator. The single `report.exporter` provider must return the complete ordered batch; core rejects malformed/partial output and owns ZIP construction. The default Markdown output preserves existing names/bytes. Single-report browser Markdown download stays local.
  - Generated sections expose backend-derived `evidence_level`/`grounded`; references may carry exact `source_id`/`element_id`. Report concurrency follows its own rails, not `KG_JOB_CONCURRENCY`.

  **"Pending analysis" excludes a source that was analysed and legitimately produced nothing.** The predicate is not "this source has no knowledge objects" — a document with very little text, or one that is entirely uncaptioned images, completes analysis with zero objects, and treating that as pending made the count un-clearable: the badge stayed 待分析 forever, the dashboard kept offering 「继续分析」, and every run re-analysed those sources at full model cost only to get zero again. A source counts as analysed-and-empty when its latest `kg` extraction run is `completed`, its message carries the zero-object marker written by the success path, and it has no failed windows and is not a partial retry. `no-llm` runs (extraction model unconfigured) deliberately do NOT qualify — those really have not been analysed, and must be picked up once a model is configured. The single authoritative statement of the predicate is `kg_analyzed_without_objects` in `backend/app/models/sources.py`; the two pending-count queries mirror it in SQL (they must be one `COUNT`) and are reconciled case-by-case against it by `backend/tests/test_kg_empty_extraction_marker.py`. Incremental analysis skips these sources; a full rebuild still picks them up, which is the path back after switching models or re-parsing with OCR.

The default report-planning rails are four retrieval directions per section,
eight direct-element candidates, and corpus-map scout widths of 12 KG records,
eight PPR chunks, and eight confirmed Memory records. They are independently
deployment-configurable through `REPORT_MAX_SUBQUERIES_PER_SECTION`,
`REPORT_PROBE_ELEMENT_LIMIT`, `REPORT_SCOUT_KG_LIMIT`,
`REPORT_SCOUT_CHUNK_LIMIT`, and `REPORT_SCOUT_MEMORY_LIMIT`; changing a scout
width changes planning context only, never the final section evidence budget.

The current persistence/API contract is the `reports` table and `/reports` APIs; retired content-studio storage and routes are not part of the current runtime.

### Deployment extensions

Deployment companion services are explicitly declared under
`extensions.<plugin_id>.services.<service_id>` in `EXTENSIONS_CONFIG`. An absent
`services` table preserves existing behavior; `enabled=false` omits that plugin's
services. `managed` services have a foreground argv command and working directory;
`external` services are readiness-checked but never started or stopped by core.
Each enabled service is required and declares exactly one HTTP or command readiness
probe. Dependency references use `plugin_id/service_id`, must name enabled services,
and must form an acyclic graph. Startup waits for dependencies and readiness before
starting the application; companion startup failure rolls back the processes created by that
attempt. Shutdown reverses dependency order. There is no optional-service degraded
mode or automatic restart.

Service lifecycle belongs to the launch scripts and the explicit
`extensions services` CLI group. Plugin import, discovery, `configure()`, ordinary
CLI/batch jobs, and the admin access toggle never spawn or terminate companion
processes. Configuration/environment changes require stop/start. Status and stop
operate on the saved run identity, including after the configuration is edited or
removed. Lifecycle output contains safe metadata only; commands, environment values,
probe responses, paths, and plugin stdout/stderr are not exposed through the admin
API or copied into supervisor logs. Author and operator instructions are in the
[extension SOP](./deployment-extensions-sop.md#companion-service-delivery-contract).

Companion-service numeric rails (seconds, finite positive numbers; booleans rejected):

| Configuration key | Default | Inclusive range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `startup_timeout_seconds` | 60 | 0.1–3600 |
| `shutdown_timeout_seconds` | 15 | 0.1–300 |
| `healthcheck_timeout_seconds` | 2 | 0.1–30 |

`GET /api/admin/extensions` is system-admin-only and returns a whitelist projection of the startup-frozen registry topology: six topology whitelist fields per extension — `id`, `version`, `trust`, `display_name`, `contributions[{id,point,kind}]`, `ui_contributions[{id,slot,capability}]` (the three runtime-toggle fields are covered in the next paragraph) — never a module path, file path, settings value, internal capability reason, or exception text; a plugin entry the deployment marked `enabled=false` never registers and so never appears here. `GET /api/system/extensions` (any authenticated user, live availability only) is unchanged.

Runtime toggle is an admin gate layered on top of that loaded topology, not a second discovery mechanism: only a loaded plugin with `trust="deployment"` can be switched, and builtin rows stay read-only forever. `GET /api/admin/extensions` adds three fields to every topology row — `runtime_enabled` (`bool | null`), `runtime_updated_by` (`str | null`), `runtime_updated_at` (`str | null`, ISO timestamp). Builtin rows are always `null, null, null`. A deployment row with no database row yet (no admin has ever touched it) reads `true, null, null` — no row means enabled — otherwise it reports the last write and who made it. `PATCH /api/admin/extensions/{plugin_id}` (body `{"enabled": bool}`) is admin-only, and a non-admin caller gets 403 with "仅管理员可管理扩展运行时开关"; it accepts only a plugin id this process currently has loaded with `trust="deployment"` — an unloaded id, a builtin id, or a typo all 404 with "该扩展不存在或不支持运行时开关". A successful write takes effect immediately in the process that handled the request (every registry evaluation in that process from then on sees the new value) and returns the written `{plugin_id, runtime_enabled, runtime_updated_by, runtime_updated_at}`; if the in-process publish that follows the write fails, the response still succeeds (2xx) — the write itself is durable, and that process converges on its next background refresh tick. Once disabled, every retrieval/parsing/UI capability the plugin contributes is unavailable to every request: `GET /api/system/extensions`'s `unavailable_reason` keeps its existing closed vocabulary — `"disabled"` now covers both an admin's runtime switch and the plugin's own probe returning `DISABLED`, indistinguishably on the wire — or `"unavailable"`; and the plugin's own HTTP routes under `/api/extensions/{plugin_id}/` return 403 with "该扩展已被管理员停用" for every request while the gate is on. Convergence is layered, not instantaneous everywhere: the process that performed the write sees it at once; other serving processes in the same deployment (additional replicas) catch up on their own low-frequency refresh tick (default interval and bounds are registered in the deployment reference); offline CLI and batch processes read the value once, at startup composition, and never again during that run. If the disabled plugin happens to be a notebook's currently selected indexing pipeline, the notebook reuses the existing missing-plugin degradation: `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/indexing-pipeline`'s `available` turns `false`, the UI offers a revert-to-builtin path, and ordinary reads of previously published artifacts are unaffected.

`/api/extensions/{plugin_id}/…` is the only mount point for a deployment plugin's own HTTP routes: a router-level session dependency means no anonymous face, and the router factory receives a nine-field `PluginRouteContext` — `plugin_id`, `settings`, `require_notebook_capability`, `require_notebook_read`, `current_actor`, `user_error`, `url_sources`, `task_stream`, `emit_event` — never the repository, global `Settings`, a model client, the FastMCP host, or a raw bearer token. **Every core port reached through those seams authorizes the request's own user itself** — e.g. `url_sources.import_urls` checks the `sources:write` capability for the calling user and 404s otherwise — so the mount's own `{notebook_id}` path-shape guard is defence in depth, not the authorization boundary. The URL import port has two call shapes for one implementation: a sync (`def`) handler is already in FastAPI's threadpool and calls `import_urls`, while an `async def` handler is on the event loop thread and must `await import_urls_async(...)`, which offloads the same blocking work (database writes plus one serial remote probe per URL) to the threadpool along with the request context, so authorization is identical on both paths. Calling `import_urls` from an async handler raises `RuntimeError` before doing any work — a developer error surfaced as a `500` with a traceback naming the method to await, never as user-facing copy. Trusted-proxy SSRF exemption (deployment-level): core's URL import refuses URLs that resolve to private/loopback addresses, which would exclude a co-deployed plugin proxy on a private origin; a deployment lists such trusted proxy origins in `URL_IMPORT_TRUSTED_PROXY_HOSTS` (comma-separated; exact origin match after lowercasing scheme/host and normalizing default ports — a different port is a different origin, the path never participates). A matching URL skips only the public-address check — in the import probe and in the parse-time download alike, the same whitelist being threaded into the parser chain so an exempted source cannot end up created-but-unparseable; URL shape checks (scheme, no credentials, port validity) still apply, and the exemption path performs no DNS resolution (a trusted proxy host may not resolve at all). The whitelist comes from deployment settings only — request input can never alter it. The browser URL endpoint and this plugin adapter both read the deployment whitelist for the import probe, so either can accept a trusted proxy's Markdown snapshot; the parse-time download applies the same whitelist to every matching URL source, reparse included and across redirects. An empty list (the default) keeps the historical behaviour bit-for-bit. `task_stream.response(request, work, stage=...)` is the separate request-local slow-work port: `work(cancellation_event)` must be synchronous, runs off the event loop, and receives a cooperative event set on browser disconnect; `stage` must be a stable lowercase code and core namespaces it with the plugin id. The response uses the shared `started` / content-free heartbeat / `final` NDJSON protocol, disables proxy buffering, and turns every worker exception into the stable `extension_task_failed` frame without exception text. It is for direct interactive waiting only, never for durable jobs; `ask.engine`/`ask.gap_consult` already run inside the durable Ask job, parser/indexing work already runs in background ingestion/rebuild jobs, completion observers run after durable commit, and `report.exporter` remains a binary response. A 401 plugin code raises — as either `fastapi.HTTPException` or `starlette.exceptions.HTTPException` (the former is a subclass of the latter; both are caught identically) — *or returns* is translated to 424 (with a logged event) so it cannot be mistaken for a dead session. "Plugin code" covers the handler **and the plugin's own `Depends(...)` callables at any nesting depth**: FastAPI solves dependencies before it calls the endpoint, so an upstream check written as a dependency — the ordinary shape — would otherwise leak a real 401 to the browser and sign the user out. Dependencies get the raised half only, since a dependency's return value is injected as a parameter and never becomes the response. Core's own dependencies are excluded by object identity *and* by defining module, so a genuine 401 from core's router-level session gate still surfaces as 401; generator (`yield`) dependencies and security schemes are left untouched.

Registered limits: the plugin observability-event whitelist accepts exactly four fields (`event`/`outcome`/`count`/`elapsed_ms`); `count`/`elapsed_ms` must be integers in `0..1e9`; a stable code (event name, outcome, or discovery/mount rejection reason) is at most 64 characters; each plugin may declare at most one HTTP route contribution. New-plugin onboarding SOP — writing the backend bundle and the build-time UI package, local integration, packaging, install, startup validation, upgrade/rollback, and the full rejection-code table: [Deployment extensions SOP](./deployment-extensions-sop.md).

For trusted-proxy imports, the private-address exemption survives only redirects to the same normalized initial origin. A redirect to another origin must satisfy the public-address check, even if that origin is separately listed.

### Source element enrichment (`source.element_enricher`)

A new production extension point lets a deployment plugin add machine-derived detail — arbitrary structured metadata, plus an optional description — to the elements one source just parsed, before they are persisted. Unlike `ask.gap_consult`, which augments an answer with material the notebook never owns, this point augments the notebook's own persisted elements: core owns the schema (`metadata.extensions[<contribution_id>]` plus an appended `description`/`text`), and a plugin only ever contributes a value into it.

**Mount.** The host runs inside `SourceIngestionService`'s per-source pipeline, after page-boundary deduplication and before the write transaction opens — the same element generation the chunk pipeline is about to read, not a later pass, so a plugin-authored description satisfies the image/figure chunk-admission gate and reaches full-text retrieval through the element's own `text` in that same commit. A deployment with no `source.element_enricher` plugin registered pays a strict no-op: no clock read, no probe call, no event.

**What a contribution sees and returns.** Every contribution receives a read-only view of every parsed element in the source — `element_type`, `location_label`, `text`, `caption`, `description`, and, for an element carrying an already-persisted image, `asset_id`/`asset_mime` — never a parser-internal metadata mapping, a repository, or settings. Image bytes are available on demand through a reader scoped to that one contribution's own turn: it holds only file paths the calling thread resolved before any plugin ran, so the worker thread performs no database access, one image can never exceed the shared MinerU per-image cap (`MINERU_MAX_IMAGE_BYTES`), and a read past that cap, an unknown element, or the end of that turn always answers `None`, never raises. A candidate names one already-shown element and carries `metadata` (JSON-shaped, key pattern `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63}$`, nesting bounded by `ELEMENT_ENRICHMENT_METADATA_MAX_DEPTH`) plus an optional `description`. On admission, `metadata` is written to `metadata.extensions[<contribution_id>] = {"plugin_id", "plugin_version", "metadata"}` on the enriched element; a non-empty `description` is appended to the element's existing `description` (`"\n\n"`-joined when one already exists); how it lands on the element's retrievable `text` depends on the element's own type — a non-structured element (image, above all, since that is what this point actually enriches) gets the description whitespace-flattened and space-joined onto existing text, while a `code_block` or `table` element keeps its line structure and gets the description appended **verbatim** after a newline, unflattened. A second contribution addressing the same element writes its own key and appends after the first, in patch order. The old (retired) contract's `caption` rewrite is not revived — a plugin never writes `caption`.

**Budget and fail-open.** Contribution kind is `CONTRIBUTOR`. The host runs a registered contribution's availability probe and its `enrich()` call together on one private daemon thread — no thread pool, no `contextvars.copy_context()` — under a single hard wall-clock deadline (`SOURCE_ELEMENT_ENRICHER_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`) covering the whole call; because this point runs inside a parse job rather than an interactive request, the default and ceiling are minutes rather than seconds. A contribution that exhausts the deadline is abandoned and ends the whole point — no later contribution starts — while a raising contribution is fail-open and skipped, and the next one still runs. Admission (element identity, metadata shape and depth, description characters, proposal count, and persisted bytes per contribution) is checked only after a contribution returns; any single violation discards that whole contribution's batch, leaving every other contribution's output untouched. On the service side, a raising host or a malformed patch likewise discards the whole batch and leaves the source's elements exactly as parsed, with a stable rejection code recorded on the ingestion pipeline's own event stream (never a settings value, a path, or an id) so an operator can tell "nothing proposed" apart from "a whole batch discarded"; an unreadable settings value, or any other exception raised while assembling the call, instead records the `enrich` stage's own `error` status alongside the exception's class name — never a rejection code, and never the exception text itself — leaving the elements unchanged the same way.

| Bound | Value |
| --- | ---: |
| `SOURCE_ELEMENT_ENRICHER_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (default; deployment-configurable, `0 < x ≤ 900`) | 120.0 |
| `SOURCE_ELEMENT_ENRICHER_MAX_PROPOSALS` (default; deployment-configurable, `1..25,000`) | 2,048 |
| `SOURCE_ELEMENT_ENRICHER_MAX_METADATA_BYTES` (default; deployment-configurable, `1,024..16,777,216`) | 1,048,576 |
| `SOURCE_ELEMENT_ENRICHER_MAX_DESCRIPTION_CHARS` (default; deployment-configurable, `1..65,536`) | 8,192 |
| `EXTENSION_OWNER_ID_MAX_CHARS` (structural, not deployment-configurable) | 128 |
| `EXTENSION_OWNER_VERSION_MAX_CHARS` (structural, not deployment-configurable) | 64 |
| `ELEMENT_ENRICHMENT_METADATA_MAX_DEPTH` (structural, not deployment-configurable) | 12 |

### Deployment Ask engines (`ask.engine`)

Result-admission degradation uses the same core-owned trace callback to append
and stream a step without `duration_ms`, immediately before the timed terminal step.
Admission work is therefore not charged to plugin time, while
live delivery, durable rows, and the final response remain append-only and
identical.

A deployment plugin may register one or more complete Ask engines. Each `PROVIDER` exposes a frozen descriptor (`mode_id`, user-facing label/description, and `requires_kg`) plus one synchronous `answer()` method. That method still runs synchronously inside the detached durable Ask worker, but the host constructs every extension `AskMode` with `streaming=true`: `/ask-modes` projects matching `streaming=true` and `streams_trace=true`, and the official browser executes the mode through `POST /notebooks/{id}/ask/stream`. The normal `POST .../ask` compatibility route remains blocking. The mode id must begin with that plugin's own id followed by `.`, and duplicate, malformed, empty, or over-limit descriptors fail startup closed. Built-in and retired ids contain no dot, while plugin ids are already unique, so the namespace prefix is the collision proof rather than a second reserved-word list.

The provider receives the current question and only three core-owned ports. `RetrievalAccessPort.search()` wraps the existing scoped candidate path: the frozen source scope and mounted-base scope reach SQLite/PostgreSQL before candidate `LIMIT`, and private-Memory projections — including the caller's own — are excluded from the plugin universe structurally: a plugin citation has no channel to carry the Memory identity the MCP private-Memory filter (the `memory:read` capability) recognizes, so Memory never enters the plugin retrieval face at all (notebook-shared Knowhow projections stay in); results expose bounded text/title/location plus a run-local opaque evidence handle, never a notebook/source/element/chunk id. `fetch()` recognizes only a handle already issued by that same port. `EngineModelPort.complete()` uses the `plugin_engine` chat workload through the normal registry, scheduler, circuit breaker, logging, and cancellation path without exposing a URL, key, raw client, or physical binding. `EngineTraceSink.step()` admits bounded generic `plugin` trace steps. Each admitted, clipped step is stored once, assigned a core-measured `duration_ms` equal to the wall-clock interval since the preceding admitted step (or engine-stage start for the first), and immediately forwarded to the durable worker's core-owned `on_trace` sink, which persists it before emitting the NDJSON `progress` event. Provider return freezes the terminal timestamp before core validates request identity, evidence handles, and citation markers. Only a passing admission publishes `扩展引擎执行完成`; provider or admission failure publishes `扩展引擎执行失败`. This timed terminal `plugin` step sits outside the provider-authored step budget; its interval covers the tail since the last admitted step, or the complete engine stage when the provider emitted none, without charging core admission latency. Consequently the frontend's existing sum of step durations represents the whole extension-engine stage without trusting provider-authored timing. The first malformed or over-budget call appends and streams one core-owned timed `扩展引擎步骤已截断` marker outside the provider budget; later malformed/over-budget calls emit nothing. No already-delivered step is mutated, so live progress, durable rows, and a successful final `AskResponse` carry the identical append-only trace. Explicit cancellation keeps the existing post-cancel trace-write gate.

`RetrievalAccessPort` also exposes a bounded KG read surface spanning the current notebook plus mounted reference libraries. `search_kg(query, k, object_types=())` runs BM25+semantic fusion over knowledge objects. `object_types` must be a `tuple`/`list` whose entries are all `str`; anything else — a bare `str` such as `"concept"` (which would otherwise iterate character-by-character rather than naming one type), a non-`str` element, or any other container shape — raises `plugin_engine_invalid_kg_request` before any budget is spent. Within a validly-shaped request, only entries naming one of `concept`/`claim`/`formula`/`procedure` survive; an unrecognized type name is silently dropped, and if the filter started non-empty but nothing recognized survives, the call returns `()` without spending budget. `kg_neighbors(evidence_key, k, edge_type="", direction="both")` expands one hop from a KG handle already issued by `search_kg`/`kg_neighbors` earlier in the same run; an element handle, a handle from another run, an empty string, or an `edge_type` outside the twelve kinds core's KG edge schema defines (`defines`/`about`/`supports`/`derived_from`/`depends_on`/`contrasts_with`/`prerequisite_of`/`part_of`/`composed_of`/`kind_of`/`used_in`/`precedes`) all return `()` at no cost, while a `direction` other than `both`/`out`/`in` raises `plugin_engine_invalid_kg_request`. In a genuinely narrowed run (`source_scope_restricted`, the channel question — not the frozen all-selected ceiling), `kg_neighbors` on an active-notebook anchor closes entirely and returns `()` at no cost: its bounded expansion carries no source predicate below its read window, so out-of-scope neighbors could consume the window and filter-after could never recover rows that were not returned — the same discipline that closes the built-in graph channels for restricted runs. Anchors in a mounted base stay open under local narrowing (the library dimension is whole-notebook checkboxes; the two dimensions are orthogonal by contract). The two calls share one budget, `ASK_PLUGIN_ENGINE_KG_SEARCH_MAX_CALLS`, independent of `search()`'s own pool; exceeding it raises `plugin_engine_kg_call_limit`. Four points define the contract a provider must respect: **(1) citability** — a KG hit's `evidence_key` is non-empty, and so may enter `citations`, only when the object carries at least one evidence binding whose source and element are still live and has a name, definition, or verbatim excerpt to actually show (the rare case where none of those exist is likewise treated as context-only); an empty-key hit ("context-only") may inform the answer's reasoning but is registered nowhere a citation or a `kg_neighbors` anchor could reach it — submitting it as a citation gets it dropped from the citations tuple and disclosed in the trailing plugin trace step, the same way a forged handle is now handled, rather than rejecting the whole answer; **(2) citation target** — a cited KG handle's persisted `Citation` opens the object's *first surviving evidence element*, never a graph node view; **(3) no edge labels or truncation signal** — `kg_neighbors` never reports which edge kind produced a given neighbor (call once per `edge_type` to attribute by edge) or whether a full page was truncated (assume it may be), and each direction is separately capped by core's own expansion limit regardless of the requested `k`; **(4) two-lane candidate routing** — an un-narrowed plugin run passes no explicit source list, so the KG seam keeps its notebook ANN + lexical fusion and applies the run's frozen ceiling at evidence hydrate (scope-less callers such as MCP get a synthesized all-selected ceiling of the same shape the browser freezes, `narrowed=false`, never producing a user-visible scope receipt); a genuinely narrowed run pushes its frozen keys and takes the source-restricted lexical lane whose predicate lands before `LIMIT`. Registered dual cost of the un-narrowed lane: the caller's own Memory-derived hits pass the ceiling, occupy candidate slots inside `k`, and are then dropped whole by the port's out-of-universe rule — a run whose top hits are Memory-derived can return fewer than `k` usable results. `kg_overview()` returns the same bounded (≤ 600 characters, `KG_OVERVIEW_MAX_CHARS`) collection-map text the built-in reasoning engine injects into its own prompt — enumerable-collection counts, the four knowledge-object type counts, and source counts for the current scope — memoized once per run (repeat calls return the same string) and not a parseable format by contract; a graph-less notebook's overview simply omits the knowledge-object line, which a provider should read as a signal to route away from the KG port. In a genuinely narrowed run the overview is suppressed entirely (empty string, no underlying count) for the same reason the neighbor channel closes: its counting seam applies only the library dimension, so it would otherwise hand a scoped run whole-notebook aggregates it may not read.

The provider returns Markdown plus an ordered tuple of issued handles. Core admits every returned handle and every `[kN]`/`【kN】` marker **per item** rather than failing the whole answer closed: only a malformed result shape — a non-`str` answer, a non-`tuple` citations sequence, or a wrong port type — rejects the whole answer, with the stable code `invalid_plugin_engine_result`; the only other whole-answer rejection is a body stripped down to nothing, described at the end of this paragraph. Within a well-formed result, a forged, cross-run, or evidence-less handle has no record in core's private ledger and therefore no evidence to show: that citation is dropped, every body marker that pointed at it is removed, and the remaining legal citations are renumbered with the body's markers rewritten to match (a marker group whose members are all illegal loses its brackets entirely, not just the illegal member inside them); a loose, marker-shaped bracket group that never matched citation-marker syntax to begin with (e.g. `[k1, nope]`) is stripped from the body the same way, but only when the group READS as a citation marker — some separator-delimited segment inside it consists solely of whitespace-separated `k<digits>` tokens, which also covers the comma-less `[k1 k2]` a model can mistype. Ordinary bracketed prose survives verbatim: `[k8s 官方文档](https://kubernetes.io)`, `[k1000 档]`, and `【定义 [k1]】` are not touched. That narrowing is load-bearing because the rule's job changed: it used to reject the whole answer (loud), and it now deletes user-visible prose in place (silent), so it has to be precise about what reads as a citation. Stripping also never mints a new marker. Removing a bracket group lets the text on either side concatenate, and that join can spell a marker-shaped group that never passed verification (`[k1[k9]2]` becomes `[k12]` once the invalid inner `[k9]` is removed, and `[k1[k9, nope]2]` reaches the same place one pass later). Verified markers are therefore held aside while residual groups are stripped repeatedly to a fixed point, and only restored afterwards. That strip runs two patterns each round, not one: the marker-like scan deliberately refuses to cross a newline (so it cannot swallow ordinary prose across paragraphs), while citation-marker syntax itself accepts newlines as inter-token whitespace, so a join such as `[k1,\n[k9]k2]` → `[k1,\nk2]` is invisible to the first pattern yet still renders and binds as a citation. Because holding the verified markers aside leaves no legal marker in the body by construction, any citation-marker match seen during stripping is necessarily join residue and is removed. Only core's own canonical `[k1]` / `[k1, k2]` forms are restored at the end, so every marker in the final body names a surviving citation — an unverified citation never reaches the user wearing a citation's appearance, unconditionally rather than merely for well-behaved input. A citation that was retrieved but never marked in the body is treated the other way: it is **kept** in the citations fallback list without producing an anchor — the same citations ⊇ anchors shape the built-in modes already use — rather than being dropped. A sanity ceiling on the citations tuple's length (`plugin_engine_citation_limit`) follows both retrieval pools — `(ASK_PLUGIN_ENGINE_SEARCH_MAX_CALLS + ASK_PLUGIN_ENGINE_KG_SEARCH_MAX_CALLS) × ASK_PLUGIN_ENGINE_RETRIEVAL_MAX_K` — since every call in either pool can issue up to the per-call `k` limit; a result over that ceiling is **truncated** to it rather than rejected (the failure code stays registered in the error-code table as a fallback mapping, but admission itself no longer raises it). Every one of these degradations is disclosed, never silent: core appends one `step_type="plugin"` step to the persisted trace (front-end label 「扩展」) with a fixed summary, 「引用核验未全部通过」, and a detail line naming each category that fired and how many entries it touched — e.g. 「2 条引用无法核验，已移除」, 「正文中 1 个引用标记无法核验，已移除」, 「1 条引用未在正文中被引用，仅列入引用列表」, 「引用条数超过本次可签发上限，超出部分已忽略」, 「正文中 N 处疑似引用标记无法解析，已移除」. Disclosure is what makes the dropping legitimate: the earlier fail-closed design's rationale was that stripping a bad anchor would let unverified prose look grounded with nothing to show for it; a visible trailing trace step closes that gap now, so an answer whose prose survives and only loses its citations still saves, with an empty citations tuple and `grounded`/`evidence_level` falling to their ungrounded/inferred defaults the same way any answer with no surviving evidence does. If stripping instead leaves nothing but whitespace — the whole answer was one unverifiable marker, so there is no prose left to keep — the result is rejected outright with the stable code `plugin_engine_unverified_citation`, whose existing fallback copy 「扩展引擎返回了无法核验的引用」 describes exactly that, rather than persisting a blank answer bubble. Core still builds `Citation` and `AnswerAnchor` from its private ledger and saves through the ordinary durable answer seam only after rechecking mode/notebook/question/conversation/actor/job/run/scope identity — that recheck, and durable-citation construction, are unchanged. MCP's `ask` applies the same per-item admission: a call no longer errors out when some citations fail verification, it returns the degraded body and only the citations that verified, and the disclosure trace step persists with the answer the same way (visible from the browser); the MCP response shape gains no new field in v1. Public conversation projection remains on its existing whitelist. v1 deliberately receives no history, intent preflight, PPR/community/graph-walk, repository, `Settings`, connection, or service locator, and Deep Report still does not reach it. Automatic UI mode hides the extension group and submits the built-in `reasoning` engine at the standard effort; advanced mode projects available engines as the third group. MCP's `ask` admits (single notebook only) the same registered, live-available mode id as its `mode` parameter, alongside the built-in `chunk`/`reasoning` — response shape (`answer_markdown` with markers normalized to `[kN]`, plus a `citations` list) matches the built-in modes, conversation history still does not enter the plugin engine, and `conversation_id` only affects UI turn grouping. A `mode` naming an unregistered id gets an error listing the currently legal mode ids; a registered-but-currently-unavailable id (an unconfigured plugin key, for instance) gets a distinct, actionable message rather than being folded into the same rejection, and a plugin-engine failure during the call itself surfaces the same way — a human-readable sentence with a parenthetical stable reason code, never a bare code or an opaque traceback. A failed `/ask-modes` read leaves all built-ins usable and retries after the next committed workspace.

| Ask-engine rail | Default | Valid range / structural cap |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `ASK_PLUGIN_ENGINE_RETRIEVAL_MAX_K` | 20 | `1..500` |
| `ASK_PLUGIN_ENGINE_SEARCH_MAX_CALLS` | 8 | `1..100` |
| `ASK_PLUGIN_ENGINE_KG_SEARCH_MAX_CALLS` (shared by `search_kg` and `kg_neighbors`) | 16 | `1..100` |
| `ASK_PLUGIN_ENGINE_EVIDENCE_MAX_CHARS` | 4,000 | `100..50,000` |
| `ASK_PLUGIN_ENGINE_PROMPT_MAX_CHARS` (also bounds a port search query) | 32,000 | `1..1,000,000` |
| `ASK_PLUGIN_ENGINE_MODEL_MAX_CALLS` | 4 | `1..32` |
| `ASK_PLUGIN_ENGINE_TRACE_MAX_STEPS` | 32 | `1..256` |
| `ASK_PLUGIN_ENGINE_TRACE_LABEL_MAX_CHARS` | 160 | `1..1,000` |
| `ASK_PLUGIN_ENGINE_TRACE_DETAIL_MAX_CHARS` | 1,000 | `1..10,000` |
| descriptor `mode_id` / label / description | — | 128 / 80 / 300 characters |
| `kg_overview()` output (`KG_OVERVIEW_MAX_CHARS`, contract bound not a deployment rail) | — | 600 characters |

### Deployment indexing pipelines (`indexing.pipeline`)

Deployment plugins may contribute notebook-scoped indexing pipelines whose ids are namespaced under their plugin id and whose descriptors expose only label, description, version, and the two override flags. Parser routing stays on the startup-frozen ProviderChain; users choose only the indexing pipeline, never a parser. `GET /api/notebooks/{id}/indexing-pipeline` is reader-visible and returns the sanitized current selection plus the notebook-local option list and booleans such as `available`, `missing`, and `pending`; it never leaks plugin paths, capability names, stack traces, or loader reasons. `PATCH /api/notebooks/{id}/indexing-pipeline` is admitted by `kg:write`, so owners and group content-managers may switch the desired pipeline while pure readers remain read-only.

The notebook settings surface is intentionally split. Owners and content-managers may edit notebook metadata and switch the indexing pipeline, but only owners may load or mutate mounted reference libraries — reading mounts is `notebook:configure`, changing them is `notebook:mount`, and both remain owner-only. Pure readers still get a read-only settings view that shows the current pipeline and status. Any pipeline change requires an explicit full-rebuild confirmation. PATCH first commits desired `(pipeline_id, version, opaque generation)`, then claims the existing durable `kg_build_jobs` rebuild single-flight and returns `pending` plus its `job_id`; the worker performs the bounded whole-notebook chunk plan, optional core-owned KG run, and eligible scale rebuild. A late worker can publish only while its exact generation still owns the selection. A failed/oversized plan leaves the desired generation pending; GET projects `rebuild_status=failed`, and notebook settings offers both same-pipeline retry and one-click builtin recovery. **Large libraries are locked out of switching to a custom pipeline (batch-3-W3, decision D3)**: when a notebook's active-object count exceeds `INDEXING_PIPELINE_SWITCH_MAX_OBJECTS` (default 200k — a dedicated threshold at the WR-2 failure scale, deliberately not the tiny copy threshold), `begin()` refuses any **non-builtin** target before persisting intent (409 with explicit copy, nothing saved, the current index unaffected). **Reverting to builtin stays allowed** — a large notebook stuck on an absent/failed custom selection has every write fail-closed by `require_write_admission`, and the builtin revert is its only self-service exit; a recovery rebuild that fails again merely returns to the retryable state. An unchanged clean-state save still short-circuits to 200 (a stuck-pending state never matches the unchanged fast path — its revert goes through the exemption instead). GET carries the server truth as `large_library_locked`; the settings panel disables only the custom-pipeline options and the same-pipeline retry button, keeps builtin recovery clickable, and explains inline. The full restructure (per-source transactions + generation-pointer publish) is deferred until real demand.

While `pending`, ordinary source upload/reparse, manual KG build, and scale rebuild writes fail closed. The worker validates bounded chunk proposals for every user-visible ingestion source, computes embeddings outside any publication transaction, and persists each source's chunks, reverse rows, vectors, KG payload, source facts, and extraction outcome into an invisible durable notebook stage. Hidden Memory/Knowhow synthetic products are core-owned, actor-scoped at read time, excluded from the selectable strategy, and never enter that stage. A malformed per-source chunk proposal degrades that source to the builtin chunker with a stable content-free warning; a whole-notebook bound breach writes no live product. A missing or unavailable selected plugin exposes a revert-to-builtin path without preventing ordinary reads of the previously published artifacts.

When `overrides_kg_extraction` is enabled, the plugin owns only a window prompt builder and model-response mapper. Core still owns windowing, the `kg_extract` workload/client and output cap, cancellation, schema admission, evidence binding, persistence, and durable job state. Core mints window-local opaque evidence handles; an unknown handle, object type, edge type, illegal endpoint pair, malformed prompt/fragment, plugin exception, or configured bound breach fails that source closed. The durable notebook job reaches terminal `failed`, but the live extraction history, source/parser status, graph, chunks, source facts, and published identity remain byte-for-byte unchanged; the failed stage is discarded. A pipeline that overrides KG cannot take the no-model success path.

Publication begins only after every staged source is complete. Before its first live mutation, the SQLite/PostgreSQL transaction revalidates the running job, desired generation, exact visible-source/element snapshot, staged source set, vector shape, endpoint closure, and source-local evidence ownership. It then replaces visible-source chunks/reverse rows/FTS/vectors and source-derived KG/facts/extraction state, invalidates notebook-derived KG products and their mutation sequences, updates only parser-independent `chunked_at`, publishes the unified identity, clears job authority, records `succeeded`, and deletes the stage in that same transaction. A no-KG/model path explicitly preserves live KG while publishing staged chunks. Failure, cancellation, startup recovery, or a late/mixed generation deletes only the stage, so readers continue to see one complete old generation until a complete new one commits.

| Rail | Default | Valid range |
|---|---:|---:|
| `INDEXING_PIPELINE_MAX_PROPOSALS_PER_SOURCE` | 2,000 | `1..100,000` |
| `INDEXING_PIPELINE_MAX_TEXT_CHARS` (proposal text and section path) | 20,000 | `1..1,000,000` |
| `INDEXING_PIPELINE_MAX_ELEMENT_REFS` | 500 | `1..100,000` |
| `INDEXING_PIPELINE_REBUILD_MAX_PROPOSALS` | 50,000 | `1..2,000,000` |
| `INDEXING_PIPELINE_REBUILD_MAX_TEXT_CHARS` | 100,000,000 | `1..2,000,000,000` |
| `INDEXING_PIPELINE_PUBLISH_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (publisher waits for in-flight admitted ingestion to drain before the atomic publish; on timeout the stage is discarded and the job fails retryably) | 600 | `0<x..3,600` |
| `INDEXING_PIPELINE_KG_MAX_MESSAGES` | 8 | `1..64` |
| `INDEXING_PIPELINE_KG_PROMPT_MAX_CHARS` | 64,000 | `1..2,000,000` |
| `INDEXING_PIPELINE_KG_SCHEMA_HINT_MAX_CHARS` | 16,000 | `0..250,000` |
| `INDEXING_PIPELINE_KG_MAX_OBJECTS_PER_WINDOW` | 512 | `1..10,000` |
| `INDEXING_PIPELINE_KG_MAX_EDGES_PER_WINDOW` | 1,024 | `0..20,000` |
| `INDEXING_PIPELINE_KG_MAX_EVIDENCE_HANDLES` | 32 | `1..1,000` |
| `INDEXING_PIPELINE_KG_MAX_STEPS_PER_OBJECT` | 128 | `0..2,000` |
| `INDEXING_PIPELINE_KG_NAME_MAX_CHARS` | 8,000 | `1..100,000` |

### Gap consultation (`ask.gap_consult`)

A production extension point lets a deployment plugin offer pointers to material **outside** the notebook when a reasoning Ask run's own retrieval came up short. Suggestions are not notebook evidence: they are not scored or bound to `[k]` anchors and cannot change the drafted answer. A separate, explicitly unverified external supplement may summarize their snippets with `[Xn]` links. Importing a URL remains an ordinary source add with its own parsing and permissions.

**Trigger.** Reasoning Ask only — deep reports and Knowhow row completion do not route through `_run_reasoning_stage` — at every retrieval effort tier, at most once per run after the response-draft stage returns and before persistence. The trigger reads only pre-draft facts: a confirmed direction left unexecuted (`intent_coverage_incomplete`), or an evidence pool (`top_hits + chunks + elements`) thinner than that tier's `ranked_final_floor`. It adds no retrieval query or model call merely to decide whether to trigger; once triggered, source selection and the optional supplement do use their own model workloads. A degraded retrieval can also satisfy the thin-evidence condition. The draft envelope contains no gap suggestions or trace, so the drafted answer cannot vary with external results.

**Source selection and egress.** A contributor may expose `describe_sources()` with `SourceDescriptor` entries (`source_id`, display name, languages, content type, query advice). Source IDs must be unique among offered sources; malformed, duplicate, unavailable or undescribed sources are not offered. The `gap_consult_query` model selects up to `GAP_CONSULT_MAX_QUERY_SOURCES` offered source IDs and up to `GAP_CONSULT_MAX_QUERIES_PER_SOURCE` phrases for each. Its input is limited to the egress-safe `question`, bounded `gaps`, and source descriptors: conversation history, notebook evidence, private identity and unreviewed style or intent rewrites are excluded. No descriptor, unconfigured/failed model, invalid or empty selection means **zero** `consult()` calls; the host never falls back to all contributors. Only selected contributors are called.

The plugin receives one bounded `GapConsultQuery`: `question` uses the reviewed final wording only after an actual clarification gate; otherwise it uses the raw question, never an auto-confirmed model rewrite. It is bounded by `GAP_CONSULT_QUESTION_MAX_CHARS`; `gaps` contains at most `GAP_CONSULT_MAX_GAP_PHRASES` confirmed but unexecuted labels, each bounded by `GAP_CONSULT_PHRASE_MAX_CHARS`. Citation markers are stripped. `source_queries` maps the selected source IDs to their bounded generated phrases; no notebook/actor/source identity or evidence appears in the call context. `AskResponse.gap_egress` persists the destinations and phrases core actually passed at contributor invocation, including zero-result or failed attempts; it is absent if no source was invoked. Core cannot inspect downstream requests made by a contributor. Each admitted suggestion may also expose bounded, contributor-reported `actual_query`; core does not independently verify that phrase. The private source ID is a routing key, not a notebook source ID.

**Budget and fail-open.** The frozen `GapConsultHost` runs a contribution's availability probe and its `consult` call together on one private `daemon=True` thread — no thread pool, so one hung plugin leaks one thread on the affected request rather than occupying a shared worker the whole deployment depends on; no `contextvars.copy_context()`, so a plugin cannot inherit this request's frozen retrieval scope, retrieval run, or a leaf-I/O fan-out slot simply by running underneath it — joined in 50ms slices against a hard wall-clock deadline (`ASK_GAP_CONSULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, default 4.0s, `0 < x ≤ 30`) that covers the **whole** call, both halves. Cancellation and that deadline are re-read on **every** pass of the join loop, the pass that observes the worker finish included: a contributor that answers *after* its budget is spent has answered late, and a late answer is abandoned exactly like a hung one — reading the deadline only while the thread was still alive would make the outcome depend on which side of the thread's death the 50ms slice happened to land. This budget is spent **before** the reader has an answer — unlike the cooperative post-completion deadlines above, every second here is a second of answer latency — hence the small default and the tight ceiling. **A genuinely hung plugin leaks one daemon thread per affected request; this is a registered, accepted cost, not a defect — a circuit breaker is deferred work.** Anything short of a clean, on-time, well-shaped response is fail-open: no registered host, a dormant point (`has_contributions()` is `False`), a malformed call context, an empty caller-supplied question (the host does not trust its own caller either — this is unreachable in practice today, since `AskRequest.question` already enforces `min_length=1` before a run's own question can reach this call site), a raising contributor, an exhausted budget, or a host answering a shape the port never promised — all return `()` and leave the answer exactly as it would otherwise have been. Cancellation is the sole exception and keeps propagating (`AskCancelled`). "Fail-open" means the answer is unchanged and no error banner or diagnostic is surfaced — it does **not** mean the `gap_consult` disclosure trace step disappears: that step's whole job is telling the reader a bounded egress attempt happened, so a contributor call that times out, raises, or returns malformed data still records that invocation with a suggestion count of `0`; failures before any contributor is invoked produce no egress receipt (a codex #584 R4 suggestion to suppress the step on failure was deliberately rejected; see `ask_service.py::_consult_gap_sources`). Sanitization — non-empty title; `url` restricted to `http`/`https` with a non-empty host and no control characters, and never truncated (a shortened URL is a silently wrong destination, so an over-long one is dropped instead); summary/source-label stripped and truncated — happens in the host, after the plugin returns, never inside the plugin. A result whose `status` is `UNAVAILABLE` contributes **nothing**, items or not: that status is the contributor's own statement that it could not serve this call, so its payload does not get to contradict it (and its URLs never enter the cross-contributor de-duplication set, so a contributor that really can serve the call is not blocked by a withdrawn link); `PARTIAL` means "some of it", not "none of it", and is still admitted. The *work* of admission is itself bounded in both dimensions — a bounded multiple of the slots still to fill is the most items ever examined, and every string is cut to its own limit plus headroom before anything walks it — so an unbounded returned payload costs a bounded scan rather than an unbounded one on the critical path, after the deadline above has already been honoured. The cut lands on plugin output, never on user data.

At host admission, a non-null `source_queries` must be a plain mapping within the query-source and per-source-phrase rails below; one malformed entry invalidates the whole query. The host does not impose a separate key-name whitelist; core's planner chooses only offered IDs before building this mapping. Descriptor fields and the supplement's source/knowledge excerpts are bounded before model input, with their public descriptor rails listed below; the supplement's internal prompt projections do not change the public response limit.

The **same** wall-clock deadline starts before `describe_sources()` and covers source discovery, the `gap_consult_query` model call, the host's availability checks and selected `consult()` calls, and `external_evidence_answer` when summaries are available. These phases do not each get a fresh four seconds. The planner itself receives at most 40% of the configured budget and cannot extend the shared deadline. Model-client lookup failure, timeout, or malformed model output/JSON leaves the drafted answer intact; no source is consulted if source selection fails.

**Availability.** A plugin declares the capability it probes through its own manifest `provides`, exactly like every other contributor kind; core adds no dedicated switch beyond the shared deployment-plugin machinery. A deployment with no `ask.gap_consult` plugin registered pays zero clock reads, zero probe calls, and emits zero events — `consult()` is a strict no-op before any validation runs.

**Import.** The suggestion panel's 「导入」 button uses the ordinary core URL-import endpoint (`POST /notebooks/{id}/sources/url`, `sources:write`; read-only members see no button). Direct PDF links remain supported. A URL whose initial origin exactly matches the deployment's `URL_IMPORT_TRUSTED_PROXY_HOSTS` may also return `text/markdown`: the probe treats that trusted proxy response as a Markdown snapshot, names it `.md`, and the parse-time download routes it through the builtin Markdown parser without MinerU. This works through the ordinary UI button as well as the plugin import port. Other origins remain PDF-only; landing and abstract pages are not imports. A redirect retains the private-address exemption only when its target stays on the same normalized trusted origin; cross-origin targets must pass the public-address check, even when separately listed. URL-shape checks remain on every hop. Rejection reasons appear by the button, and a full notebook disables import before probing.

**Non-evidence, end to end.** `AskGapSuggestion` (`title`/`url`/`summary`/`source_label`/`actual_query`, no notebook evidence ID, score or citation key) lives on `AskResponse.gap_suggestions`, filled by core **after** the response draft returns. The optional `external_evidence_answer` workload uses nonempty suggestion summaries and bounded notebook excerpts to create a separate `AskResponse.external_evidence` section (`text`, structured `conflicts` with notebook claim, outside claim and note). Its `[Xn]` markers refer to original suggestion positions, link to those URLs and show their titles on hover; missing positions stay plain text. The UI marks the section unverified and displays conflicts separately. Neither suggestions nor this section alter the answer, `[k]` citations, `anchors`, `grounded`, `evidence_level` or coverage. `gap_egress`, suggestions and the supplement persist for reopened private answers but are omitted from the public conversation projection. The `gap_consult` trace step (front-end label 「外扩」) records the trigger and suggestion count without the question or URLs; the optional supplement has its own 「外部补充」 step.

| Bound | Value |
| --- | ---: |

| `GAP_CONSULT_MAX_SUGGESTIONS` | 8 |
| `GAP_CONSULT_MAX_QUERY_SOURCES` | 4 |
| `GAP_CONSULT_MAX_QUERIES_PER_SOURCE` | 2 |
| `GAP_SOURCE_DISPLAY_NAME_MAX_CHARS` | 40 |
